column1: If the problem continues, ask the recipient to tell their email admin about the problem, and give them the error (and the name of the server that reported it) shown below. It's likely that only the recipient's email admin can fix this problem.

This error occurred because a message was sent to an email address hosted by Office 365, but the address doesn't exist in the receiving organization's Office 365 directory. Directory Based Edge Blocking (DBEB) is enabled for dowlingcapitalpartners.com, and DBEB rejects messages addressed to recipients who don't exist in the receiving organization's Office 365 directory. This error is reported by the recipient domain's email server, but most often it can be fixed by the person who sent the message. If the steps in the How to Fix It section above don't fix the problem, and you're the email admin for the recipient, try one or more of the following:
Check that the email address exists and is correct - Confirm that the recipient address exists in your Office 365 directory, is correct, and is accepting messages.
Synchronize your directories - Make sure directory synchronization is working correctly, and that the recipient's email address exists in both Office 365 and in your on-premises directory.

Check for errant forwarding rules - Check for forwarding rules for the original recipient that might be trying to forward the message to an invalid address. Forwarding can be set up by an admin via mail flow rules or mailbox forwarding address settings, or by the recipient via the Forwarding or Inbox Rules features.

Make sure the recipient has a valid license - Make sure the recipient has an Office 365 license assigned to them. The recipient's email admin can use the Office 365 admin center to assign a license to them (Users > Active Users > Select the recipient > Assigned License > Edit).

Make sure that mail flow settings and MX records are correct - Misconfigured mail flow or MX record settings can cause this error. Check your Office 365 mail flow settings to make sure your domain and any mail flow connectors are set up correctly. Also, work with your domain registrar to make sure the MX records for your domain are set up correctly.
For more information and additional tips to fix this issue, see this article <https://go.microsoft.com/fwlink/?LinkId=532972> .

column2: USYD issues your electronic confirmation of enrolment (eCoE) – Your eCoE will be issued and sent to you via email within 2-3 working days of you having completed all of the necessary steps in the acceptance of offer process.
You submit a visa application to the Department of Home Affairs – Information to point you in the right direction to start this process will be provided when your eCoE is issued.

column1: We can still continue to eCoEs into early June if need be.  We just don’t recommend students to wait until then to finalise their acceptance of offer process unless they have no other option other than waiting until early June.  This is mainly due to the fact that we (USYD) cannot predict how long the visa application process will take for a particular student’s sitaution and the best guidance we can give is to finalise your acceptance of offer as soon as you can to allow as much time as possible for your visa process.

Please be reassured that the units of study you list in the application form is just your initial requests.  At USYD, students can continue requesting approval for additional units of study from the time of application until the end of the first week of classes for the semester.  It’s totally normal that students will usually request a few additional units between application stage and start of classes due to change of mind, updated advice from their home institution, etc.

We have several thousand units of study across many Faculties and Schools.  You can find a master list of all Undergraduate-level units of study here: https://goo.gl/gKgSh5 <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fgoo.gl%2FgKgSh5&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cbfd2a236c38c4acd91a208deb4a211df%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639146805639845471%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=9GEWTVoDD2%2BsrxJnMBKcFpb4zhfhKcXZE4eSRRSqAF4%3D&reserved=0> .  Make sure to focus your requests on units of study listed as being offered in ‘Semester 2’ or ‘Both Semesters’.  If you come across any other units of study you’d like to request here at USYD please send me an email to let me know the unit code + name for each unit of study you are requesting.  NOTE: Any unit of study requests received close to or during my time away will be followed up ASAP after I return to work.
Next steps in June and July

When I am back from my break, we will have several exciting topics to share with you including the enrolment task, our pre-departure information, class timetables and more!  Here at USYD our systems and processes work a bit differently than most students are used to and I am here to help guide you through these key topics in preparing for your program with USYD.
I look forward to hearing from you soon!
Kristin Johnson | Senior Study Abroad Adviser

column1: Good morning. Let’s talk about what happens when countries say they’re going to stop shooting at each other.
The site of an Israeli airstrike in Beirut’s southern suburbs this month. Daniel Berehulak/The New York Times

There was a three-day truce last week in the Russia-Ukraine war. A cease-fire in the Iran war continues, though President Trump said it was on “massive life support.” Israel and Hezbollah are still firing on each other despite their cease-fire. Nothing seems to move the needle toward peace.

Cease-fires in the age of Trump “have become a tool of performative diplomacy, stand-alone commodities used to manage media cycles while the machinery of war grinds along,” writes Marc Santora <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fnewsletter%2FS-H7mNZTUsfOW_b37MPJeQ~~%2FAAAAARA~%2F2MA2AsCbRrJDXSx_mkomtqgOo7i5Ps7AnG8vqyWRHSFOKB-CQ7tBWHriI7oKGZcoA9T-EvwUm5jZi3vwqFB9S7jj94T6nTQdVypkmfNcO62lkMnMCKsh92I5_rS01YUWJDK_Msa11f78aqZsYgi2lCldn_x9ijCTP0xQXnF6VdvZPChim2A6yh1MZBD3118DWCZpdY3ZqYnyoSRXQ2P_CGnjxbjGMfEHOOrrwHG1IEGvJRJtcqwKBoIpjyHhbqDzWf9HdVWfNoGLQOw3ZugMjsl6eh1P-iJX-fkzzsiFla8SwNhGET5xsTMxAMPhxoG4bCNZSjvJzKPPk0-J3h4D7O3jRcbZ2d7w0ehYEfGCKmfs57eQ9ElE44nodVmMChFg&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C53218fdf18cb41427b9008deb4cb9b56%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639146983758407988%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=m6Qw187HePw0aa9lEQBcSOAFBOVC5p166mCAOtZw7Ys%3D&reserved=0> , who covers the Ukraine war. A cease-fire looks like peace, and it’s good for headlines. And it’s better when fewer people die. But it doesn’t solve the underlying conflict.

And is peace even the goal for leaders in these conflicts? Linda Kinstler wrote about that <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fnewsletter%2FRQVanmMTvvjSCjwMx5eH-Q~~%2FAAAAARA~%2FUGr_gcU3kwhtYQrQOWUtImeTqn4wpQY3zRdZrgJDFAfALrAsn1-7mgVfXkFZ1jx3cziyvQeZxc63NtggiP94SLAJcQlXoEYDAzilOtTzsjwctEWFDnEIWDIAn8yorLHYAwAPCe3p4vi2hq_By24o3O-1rIh-RqIb5MGaOCW0m8ocKupUF8f8rMz9ph2ev9YIVDnVTzWYyFXpK-AO2kqHmh0Wikv_Pe7Xni-Sn7OMygO2crgbwn-iuE8AYfresIZhHgem4eDFfkFJtmy-KuDE8d-Ifirv5TZEI9zFZyZMegt6uZgnbok3qsfqXqBK5AlxjipA6f7dASjv5itLQYWYHcTAg1F4zLh1KoBnUNNv361qImYWq9SKb1YXbGrftvLZHPvcDPt8QR8oLjdsxAHphg~~&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C53218fdf18cb41427b9008deb4cb9b56%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639146983758423077%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=JNjocW5EMss3BzWHGAL%2B%2F29pF6UOGP296m8jTob%2FW%2BM%3D&reserved=0>  for The New York Times Magazine last year. By using cease-fires, she asked, “have world leaders avoided difficult conversations about the origins of wars and the possibility of justice, and left the entire world less stable?”
So how seriously should we take these stopgaps? I asked Marc if cease-fires were helping in Ukraine. Here’s what he told me:
Ukrainian soldiers training in April. Brendan Hoffman for The New York Times

The fighting at the front never stopped, and at midnight Monday, as the truce technically expired, Russia resumed its bombardments of towns and cities across Ukraine. Ukraine also resumed its strikes aimed at the Russian oil industry and military production facilities.

Russia’s bombardments often combine attacks on military targets with strikes aimed at purely civilian targets. It blew up an apartment building in Kyiv last week and by Friday, rescue workers had recovered the bodies of at least 24 people, including two children.
Same as it ever was. Dread continues in Israel, where I tracked down David Halbfinger, our Jerusalem bureau chief. Life there is precarious right now, he said:

In Israel and Gaza, it’s hard to talk about cease-fires with a straight face, or at least without an ironic tone, given that Israeli airstrikes are killing Palestinians almost every day in Gaza, Hezbollah drones are targeting Israeli soldiers and one Israeli division said it killed 60 Hezbollah militants in Lebanon just over the past week. There may not be Iranian missiles hitting Israel, and Israelis in the center and south of the country may not be running to shelters. But for all anyone knows that could change even before you publish this newsletter. I’m sure everyone prefers this to whatever a war would be by comparison, but it ain’t peace, either.
Israeli strikes on a building in central Gaza on Friday. Saher Alghorra for The New York Times
Euan Ward, who lives in Beirut and covers Lebanon, spoke in a similar vein:

Lebanon’s cease-fire exists mostly on paper. In the south, I can hear the fighter jets roaring overhead and the thud of Israeli airstrikes in the distance, while evacuation warnings for entire towns remain a daily occurrence. On the country’s highways, there is always the fear that a nearby vehicle could be hit. Even in Beirut, the Lebanese capital, the constant whir of Israeli surveillance drones punctuates a fragile sense of normalcy. Lebanese authorities say hundreds of people have been killed since the truce took effect. Hezbollah, meanwhile, continues to broadcast propaganda videos of attacks on Israeli forces, including drone footage with a macabre, almost Hollywood-like quality. This is not a war that feels over.

It seems like wars don’t end any longer, and cease-fires don’t stick, Linda wrote. They become permanent only “if they are accompanied by real political compromises from both sides. Otherwise, the brief reprieve they deliver may turn out to be hardly a reprieve at all.”
In Washington. Alex Kent for The New York Times

column1: What’s the status of the “new” Air Force One? | Cleo Reilly | Hartford, Connecticut
Eric Lipton, an investigative reporter in Washington, replies:

Trump has watched with frustration as a Boeing project to replace the two jets used as Air Force One has dragged. (They won’t be ready until at least 2028.) So the Air Force is rushing to retrofit a luxury jet that the Qatari government donated by this summer, as a temporary stand-in. An Air Force spokeswoman declined to say how much it would cost — it is at least $400 million. The plane has been inspected to find hidden devices that might be used to spy on the president, and it needs to be painted with a new design Trump picked out. It’s unclear what typical protective measures — such as hardening the electrical systems against the pulse from a nuclear attack — the Air Force might decide to do without. What is certain: It will have high-end luxury accommodations Trump covets, since it was originally built for the Qatari royal family.

Plus, a private-lending value trap and suspicious betting in Washington

Good morning, I’m filling in for Spencer Jakab today. It doesn’t look like markets are ready to shake off Friday’s jitters. column1: In recent years, retailers have faced endless supply-chain challenges. Now comes the Iran war.

Retailers are starting to report results for their fiscal first quarter, which spans February through April. That means it included two full months of the conflict. The disruption will be a test early into the tenures of the newly minted CEOs at Walmart and Target, both of which report this week.

Both executives are longtime employees who have taken the helm at pivotal moments. Target is in the middle of a turnaround effort <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45756597.489321%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cud3NqLmNvbS9idXNpbmVzcy9yZXRhaWwvdGFyZ2V0LXRndC1lYXJuaW5ncy1xNC0yMDI1LWQ4MDBjODY0P2VhZnNfZW5hYmxlZD1mYWxzZSZtb2Q9ZGplbU1hcmtldHNBTQ%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dBc07fa1a7&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C437f1af13fac4a0d692e08deb4c89cfd%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639146970899224474%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=Whm%2BchlXCm5WptjAP4jmXZk8kABt1%2BIxRdBQCHSciHc%3D&reserved=0> ; Walmart is proving out <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45756597.489321%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cud3NqLmNvbS9idXNpbmVzcy9yZXRhaWwvc2hvdWxkLXdhbG1hcnQtcmVhbGx5LWJlLXRyYWRpbmctbGlrZS1hLXRlY2gtY29tcGFueS04NjMyOTM0OD9lYWZzX2VuYWJsZWQ9ZmFsc2UmbW9kPWRqZW1NYXJrZXRzQU0%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dBafcc423e&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C437f1af13fac4a0d692e08deb4c89cfd%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639146970899239563%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=H56mXE1VWI9drYwHQPSBBqqdsNXmO%2F3pKaLfcBSFwZ8%3D&reserved=0>  tech-like growth. Investors like the stories. Target and Walmart shares are up 24% and 18% this year, respectively, outpacing the market.

Gas prices could get in the way, though. Walmart executives, speaking at a Citi sector conference in March, said gas prices close to $4 a gallon cause consumers to trade down to cheaper options. Prices at $5 a gallon become more of a shock, according to a note from the bank.
Nationwide retail gas prices have hovered close to $4 a gallon since April and have been closer to $4.50 since May.

But there is a counterweight. Tax-refund season was particularly generous because of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Americans in aggregate received 18% more in refunds than they did a year earlier, according to Steven Shemesh, equity analyst at RBC Capital Markets. This translates to roughly $50 billion of additional dollars circulating in the economy.
In other words, retailers’ top lines for the quarter aren’t likely to show much damage from the Iran conflict.

The bottom line might be different. In aggregate, retailers in the S&P 500 have expanded margins over the past few years, even during stretches of high inflation. Last year, the group’s operating margins were at their highest levels since S&P Global Market Intelligence started tracking the data in 2006.
Now, prices are rising for everything from fertilizer, plastics, aluminum and fuel, potentially squeezing margins.

For Walmart, the bottom line matters because its tech-like growth story, which has helped catapult its share price to 43 times forward earnings, is predicated on growing operating profits faster than revenue. Much of this is thanks to high-margin revenue sources such as advertising and membership fees.
Rising costs could undermine that growth. Last week, Walmart said it would cut or relocate about 1,000 corporate workers.

Retail giants like Walmart, Target and Costco, which reports later in the month, are better positioned than most in a rising price environment. They tend to have bargaining power with suppliers, sell necessities and are seen as value destinations. Target’s decision to invest in groceries seems prescient.
Still, the longer the Strait of Hormuz remains closed, the harder it will be for retailers to hold the line on margins.

(Check it out and apply soon if it interests you! <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fprofellow.krtra.com%2Fc%2FylTVZRQ23pCp%2FMGoG9&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cb609f4b62d524e37e96108deb4101973%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639146178419772220%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=X9EB%2FAL3PL4Sr3kZu%2BzWhmqC5Vz6Wmb3t7KsJp15nLI%3D&reserved=0> )

I was inspired to host this program because I see so many people in my network struggling to get a job. I also noticed that few people stuck in a long-term job hunt don’t try out entrepreneurship. When I ask why, people tell me it’s too hard to get started, or it would take up too much time, or it just isn’t what they trained for.

But when employment options are scarce (and they may be for the next several years), it can be life-saving to have more options for making money. This is why learning how to create your own products and services to sell is a valuable skill that everyone should develop. And today there are so many free and low-cost tools to launch a business, you don’t need a lot of money to start one.
Building a profitable, salary-sustaining business is hard and can take some time. But getting started in entrepreneurship is pretty simple.
🍎 The key to success in entrepreneurship is to leverage the assets, perspectives, and talents that are unique to you.

My daughter Liv, who is 8, is a budding entrepreneur. She loves to make origami and decided to start selling origami door-to-door with her older brother. I loved that they would be outdoors practicing their pitch skills and getting to know their neighbors, but I didn’t feel too confident they would make much money selling folded paper animals. I thought they would face a lot of rejection and come home disappointed (but a lesson worth learning, I thought).
Boy, was I wrong! An hour later, they came home with $38 to split between the two of them 🤯.

The next time they went out, I accompanied them so I could take a peek at what they were doing. Their primary customer was not the busy mom or teenager who answered the door, but retired people. One gray-haired woman who opened her door couldn’t help but exclaim how cute they are and what a pleasure it was to meet two children from the neighborhood. She patiently listened to their pitch and product presentations, then went inside to find her wallet. “What can I purchase for $10?” she said, smiling. Liv cut her a package deal and gave her 3 of her best pieces that she had priced at $5 each. The woman thanked them profusely and invited them to come by again anytime. She told them, “You remind me of my grandchildren.”
That’s when it occurred to me. My kids weren’t selling origami, they were selling joy.
My daughter Liv manning an origami stand on our block.
Now, if I tried to sell origami door to door, it wouldn’t work. I just don’t have the cuteness factor that would bring a retired person joy.
But there are other things I could sell that might work. I could sell a creative writing class for seniors. Or sell postcards with my original watercolor paintings.
I won’t know what works until I try — and I will probably face a ton of uncomfortable rejection in the process — but I will be doing, learning, and improving until I get it right.
And let's face it — there's no good excuse not to try. If an 8-year-old can do it, so can anyone!

If you’re curious about entrepreneurship, ask yourself: What could I sell? What product or service would leverage my unique talents, skills, and ideas? And what is holding me back from pitching my product or service to someone who needs it?

Even if your new business doesn’t make much money to start, the exercise of starting a business helps you build skills in product creation, design, marketing, and sales, which are skills valuable in any industry. It also helps you meet people and build networks in your local community. And best of all — you now have something to put on your resume other than a gap.

This year, that question sounds like a dare. Neither the manicured grass nor the dignified tune of “Pomp and Circumstance” can mask the sour vibes. Inflation is accelerating. Hiring is glacial. Businesses are petrified by wars, tariffs and artificial intelligence.

Gather the evidence, and the verdict seems clear: These poor graduates are screwed. A small army of internet essayists promotes this view, and young Americans subscribe to it. Just 43 percent view their job prospects positively <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fa%2FU6_AREOttuTfQ3-D_oiQgA~~%2FAAAAARA~%2FmdbQFzFbRr-q7vcKrWLpZ4Iwo5bXesI-wR02X-MRwaPMAOzVmuztWfIrycWQvUguGPlod7CF2rBhNmuQzOjcMQQwUrX-V51YtqUztqAHwAXAHID2cGbfuiWSfZpE_3hszjZURtpXR4_sB9rzaUFT71DVlf42XaTqmBorDcsrmh_eStgtDRvE4xnD3Tw_jni67aw-mFrufbRKuJAXRcqAuuXYzSRCPh_VOpLCRVSa0FuSuhPffleepmPt-eGGinz6aF9rq5XhGh6uIg_CbuVSLf7zJrEXTF9N7xnYDUz82vNJ3Hn24dAeNTIxZJ4iNbIdo64Q5F7iSdGlt2QLipvWLhfNVtYyYYG1VseXJbpohQY8WIeTxtRiTyabk1oaVd19hSAklPD2t6o8Fi9VVJHr_A~~&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cf8c56858f2b64f6b08d208deb4080f61%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639146143928395846%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=ryatcuiFIsXoRqPo91%2BunGshil9SMKCcXKNMSQRu3Uw%3D&reserved=0>  — down from 75 percent in 2022.
Pessimism rules. But is everything as bad as it seems?

In 1965, the Who sang “The Kids Are Alright.” Thirty years later, a California band called the Offspring recorded its own take, “The Kids Aren’t Alright.” For my generation, the second song is more resonant. Its title has become a Gen-Z rallying cry.

We came of age during a recession and doom-scrolled through a pandemic. We were told that college was a shot at deliverance. If we worked hard, and if we could stomach the cost (or more often, if our parents could <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fa%2FMyyH3UL0kbthKScPOmqQeA~~%2FAAAAARA~%2F2qNYoEJvmiDbcr8vTyNX1wYxHM_z9n7dsjS1CftsZE7Lh3_Ad-MX3e7ARsEWNyb1_5Oh0ywG8nBKpIDftb5GlHX8LoKcEpt8r9zZ63YxnhPtDgPmfDBqx5KhKSQqB0boA5KmdXr6fBIY_jrS4sArcGHHe3-zka_NQwSp5MXGhIqgoTNl16xy9hauvmSK6bMTVxOypVzgONk7WlTmYnoo8IbmWhZu-Qojo0ZzFh2JOauCzdHY3QruAH9Snpk3DNGDatQqBQHxNiJInMOTjjrm1IHyguAu4Zi2Gdz5Qk9e__pQzIByrIUIBMs4vGovFpM3lUqO8KlMUT26yi-E3D_bax921TzHFX_aSA4QWLrOCckL9bJH5IxQzBaYs4irnUqmgmZjuISxbCMhJBMcdARDgjlJt426UfHfADy6u9V2ufU~&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cf8c56858f2b64f6b08d208deb4080f61%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639146143928409939%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=BqtnNr6rMBt%2BX88kJ3tcRJ%2BBN4VXHC%2BVDtOFCqNFeT0%3D&reserved=0> ), then we’d reap long-term benefits.

But for many, deliverance hasn’t come. As older Americans steered more teenagers to college, the job market for degree holders failed to keep pace. The employment rate has sagged to virtually the same dismal level <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fa%2FxhJwzBQxTeCbuGUO2Q6uhA~~%2FAAAAARA~%2FxKwc9r5pXJmf9WwZ9jWm8DraH29OEf2t1Hbe9eEsncsb-Wl3O0HbIMxGwFqV8uZ-xPkjNboIPdEG-HkyYDi6EvuxWT528fi0PFxaEcVBELtBBu4qYRxnpWPvnXonin_Jpl8arjb9VfMSTVHQnkbGMjqH37ZSpn2ZOhZBGHUQmZVDjScgNXNKkFbpzFVE2qadByXh1NxV82So6Jp20X98FXcjzvwi9n0InshO3dRaj_4uJAwZ7Bvj9tf3MkVH-cHTvT27iOyWfreJZZPaRIuYqrurHi2y5bTyAH8mh51XwNlXhUIvJCPFE6IJLWMjXJZQkLS37cGrn_acoEqEPd8HM7Sca4RK1aj2_2ym_Wfgcy0~&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cf8c56858f2b64f6b08d208deb4080f61%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639146143928425487%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=UJzg9%2F6vVGyfmp%2FpWhhq9iPAriwH1Xh9wmbDnEHFOT8%3D&reserved=0>  for young adults with and without degrees. One data point captures the disappointment: For decades, fresh grads were less likely to be unemployed than the average worker. That’s not true anymore, according to the New York Fed.
James Talarico delivering the commencement address at Paul Quinn College. Desiree Rios for The New York Times

Commencement speakers are in the unenviable position of having to acknowledge these issues without bumming everyone out. The Morning analyzed 50 graduation speeches — half from this year, half from 2018 — to see how their messaging has changed. While many of the 2018 speeches focused on gender and racial inequality, this year’s focused more on generational inequality and grit.

A third of the 2026 speakers explicitly mentioned “resilience,” but only one said that word in 2018. James Talarico, the Democratic Senate candidate in Texas, told graduates at Paul Quinn College this month that the economy simply isn’t built for Gen Z. “Young people can’t afford to buy a home,” he said. “Young people can’t afford to fill up their gas tank.”
When things get hectic, people tend to delay big decisions. Businesses do the same, which helps explain what’s happening in the labor market.

“Think about young college grads like an investment: You pay now and you get the full benefit later,” David Deming, a Harvard economist and undergraduate dean, told me. “Companies are much less likely to make those investments when the environment is so uncertain.”
Executives don’t know whether they’ll wake up to a huge trade deal with China or a complete decoupling. They don’t know whether energy prices will rise or fall.

Throw A.I. into the mix, and things get even hazier. Experts can’t agree on how this technology might change the economy, but it menaces the white-collar professions that so many students were told to pursue. Commencement speakers this year couldn’t stop talking about it. Graduates understand the threat: When a speaker at the University of Central Florida called A.I. “the next industrial revolution,” they booed <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fnewsletter%2FlkenL3y5s04RUYclyhVfeg~~%2FAAAAARA~%2FD6vgImwYtVD08QcQVWXE32adHQBa9tHvVq1kuc91yFxdmuDdSg5Xyhfgnwp-Q5FG0OzJmjbXoBxw3Ayan67v3rwMpNz6b-_M5Ynzp3nYBIfbsKw27l6XZilc7UI97EON6wx1r1AwCNDV4PHMv44bIz97vhwVo89w58penPg0prIQAazSH7LSDAxf5jbcoUeiq0wHldUc0_WVa_9WNAxXYtX2IitzoOoxXs3ODaI-vsGR4cr1JKcWEZT3pe4i-qtp9Qw9hyqL_VkqdKeaquSQESh9XDfBYBPYLjm1legVvQphhmaTHeqFyn6cwk6opKJiw_58I-dcUjqYcoO7VjXLxJ7BqhipntgC736Uk5OYZfRrVkB50STdYo6395MJ4ZiecAjoJWQReKmvpzzyvpOW6g~~&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cf8c56858f2b64f6b08d208deb4080f61%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639146143928440458%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=p5Cz8dlJXcyWx8iWFK0DNlTL%2FcAuVERAjvpTG1vuk%2BQ%3D&reserved=0> .
It’s easy to succumb to gloom, but the post-college job market isn’t all bad.

Real wages have grown a lot — more than 13 percent since 2014. Young people enjoy higher incomes <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fa%2FpTg1WqMYYeqV7Zfd9vs4Pg~~%2FAAAAARA~%2F53jfDl0wzgrIiIP6_7DzgCdlVqvlW8iFGMcqjqNVhWKEaLtR5M8RAB6mSHCwhhxuxDgpbv8fs5qm1de8TjPr4aSbRzGdeVrV54SK6XvrzkfV8v64bJFgWTgwxmaYiRl-eUTpwaZwHIomh58jm8wONtHgt9R3dQJ7v8C3JjGTFk2ZRtVgjjHvnnjtv5rfDE-XME4gBNTFWL4ELzXbe7ILnWcsTjhFWDTpxTmX7kz1b5KmKAWiplAx9ZX0aA_XA41HhgZWRl65BVwfvNlC9kTJotJDlEccTx8cwCPb7elo3m0v6aTdPlZL4VBgpkIrWVBtYFdo4LM7IFyfjzwgz796u5GiksSNaJRVJ5M-b3RfF7nZz27udBnc_dR37iDEyBkTAqPy_2BdBa-RPO1uHCDAbwN6_V6100fTs-N38m0DPUg~&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cf8c56858f2b64f6b08d208deb4080f61%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639146143928460171%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=kWQN7MF5v3aQtj5kC1iELvwjAoY6MqAU%2BFeLOOJD7Xc%3D&reserved=0>  than their parents and grandparents did, even in fields exposed to A.I. In fact, people in those fields earn more than anybody else <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fa%2FGwjnl2IcewLV_JmA4OaS-A~~%2FAAAAARA~%2FNPH4R3L-earmA2Flw1Y6_bc-hxbjGjYh1k4HAFOiqbY1teEKMFbrhYAusHIivIOdMnrLj7Od8ETEZ9TvSeuz6bksOg5GbaY6qqvMP4nhCygyFpIxV0GRGsoEbi6YW8uW91ULuZUPqHBVLNIUtz3PE13mYZ6AcBGz9Qk9y_6l9bI-UpSWBGx_QbHWOEZytJ74V7dlvnoZnZdxrL4rq3iivI1HaUn_j8XxLH-6hOeSo8m3S_YH5e7vLkGpNMr4kv_jnppPgVV3EyvGdG7m1lffw-VWUzhfNOwcQHSt5m5jT-CgiIoOjps9OHDInzyPCmjTj4sUFqSKlJx0r3L69iT-lFG84RsMLQnt7qo6l9DXAy3nz6eh0gbQxLnhmuHAfb9l&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cf8c56858f2b64f6b08d208deb4080f61%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639146143928478633%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=7MtIN0rBmbpMxZls101HdRJi%2B%2BH85FXHAbFkmkeDVT0%3D&reserved=0> .
“Graduates are still in a much better position than non-college workers, and this bears repeating early and often,” said Lisa Kahn, an economist at the University of Rochester.

Young people are saddled with debt, which postpones wealth accumulation, but as they reach their late 20s, they’re getting much richer <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fa%2FSC4TeV52Z5qHAmHIEVzeTQ~~%2FAAAAARA~%2F87vKW33j9EjFFiDVojyKLscgdtODU0BghvsDQa6v5giFyS1ilKiClXyhGHIsjSDZCuR-fNempwtjfRwk6rtCB6YFC3re296hI1m1SARM7W7F2KtFZPOXfM9POC87WBzX6WYS8VPJGJRMRCN9vnZX4-dgFeh4sBdmxDQFS8kfVXVrrlV90fg8wXN9s2tmDuwrQDhclMttchXeuCNbMP3BN4-cc2NDpZVTTnXAKK-Swy7V5FDW5g2SYkfFUnVt_a27pjcPeutklLcc_-WgRRgjzPeJ_bApLFKRVFbbmKPCNg3ijjd15aReOlSFh-JjyDiYGFKqNa6KwxkBV0x0nfldm-2eMHWj_64w_Jkq-cYXpC-65mr8-Jctwzydmr0YMRWXXdqoVwAdVvvIBpbOzL3nTQ~~&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cf8c56858f2b64f6b08d208deb4080f61%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639146143928498995%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=0ULwBH3shoJKTwUFPhRGFjsFtJSy3hqUBQmN1r%2BPi8w%3D&reserved=0>  than previous generations did at the same age, according to data from the Fed. The average net worth for millennials and Gen Z at age 30 is around $118,000. For Gen X, after adjusting for inflation, it was $53,000.
“In terms of earnings and income,” said Kevin Corinth, an economist who advised President Trump during his first term, “Gen Z is starting to pull away from previous generations.”

Some are working as servers and baristas, or in other positions that don’t require college degrees.

The hiring process feels impenetrable. My colleague Jodi Kantor recently published a book offering advice to new college graduates. Here’s one of her tips for figuring out what career you might want to pursue:

column1: Look to your friends instead. Think about what roles you take on with them: math tutor, party planner, psychologist, workout coach. These answers often reveal truths that our résumés do not. In social relationships, we aren’t bound by suffocating expectations about our future. Our friends have needs, and by noticing how we respond to them, we can learn who we are.

column1: “The Calamity Club” by Kathryn Stockett: In this long-awaited follow-up to “The Help,” Stockett tracks a plucky orphan and a resourceful spinster doing whatever it takes to survive the Great Depression in Mississippi. Both yearn for family and find it in unexpected places. One devises an ingenious plan to open a brothel with a “slapped-together band of misfits,” while the other proves unsinkable under the most trying circumstances. At more than 600 pages, “The Calamity Club” is a commitment — but, as our reviewer wrote, “It’s all about plot, baby.”

column1: This week’s subject for The Interview is Maine’s presumptive Democratic Senate nominee, Graham Platner, a progressive 41-year-old military vet and oyster farmer who is pitching a working-class revolution. He is poised to take on the incumbent, Susan Collins, in November.

You grew up in a small town, didn’t graduate college, became a bartender. But also your father was an attorney, your grandfather was a Cornell-educated architect, quite well known. How do you think about class? Is working-class how you grew up or how you live now?

I work with my hands. I don’t make a lot of money. My wife and I work incredibly hard and we probably make, like, $60,000 a year combined. We don’t have money left over. We’re not saving for retirement. I was lucky. I got to buy my house in 2017, and I could not afford my house today. My house has gone up almost three times in value.

My father gave me the mortgage, except, of course, because he’s my dad and he’s an attorney, he gave me a significantly higher interest rate than the bank would have. I could have used a V.A. home loan if I had wanted to, but at that point it was just easier to do it that way. But I could never get that today because I couldn’t afford the monthly mortgage if it was three times what it is. My income hasn’t gone up three times. But you know, in this day and age, you are working class if you make your money from work and wages. The world of wealth disparity has become so intense that there are just so many people now who are sitting on so much money who do not work. They make money off their investments. I know it’s an expansive definition of “working class,” but I think you need to have an expansive definition when we have the most expansive margin of wealth inequality in the history of the country.

I appreciate a sincerely delivered secular sermon exhorting me to go in the direction of my dreams, but, like any liberal arts grad, I insist on my own specialness, and the generic nature of graduation speeches often leaves me skeptical. “The world is more malleable than you think,” Bono <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fa%2FM_8vCYvMTEB7bAyjrZRoRQ~~%2FAAAAARA~%2F5-W-pToMbyzPJNqdmCSyiX41AvV_BK5WYLAMyC-NE6caqUiu6sZumzrVtPKq_TPoqOCw3bZA1A3lYOSnj6cipawozpuZ_jMPhx8v5w2QYkEPLnWo9OKXqo9KVvdkrzhtc_mQq2qkiDo-SvE6c99R-HSLDnO4shqCygt16Pjr3G579cynDm0H3OpoYpIFD7g5SuqCNmpHgHiAxhSXkYhDVV-YObDogkr6FIkq2u1eHzHaVXhY837TgwGZPLsoK_oZRBZt3qJ0pZa4BnCCQe_naWdF5Db1UIQCZb9Z_wyoQEFNfmnd6jk9I6pPZVOFhxdPkG4-OKHGXAht-LsLau-zYTYwhvmBH7Sxn8mPGRxD-Xo~&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cbe58141735e04683031f08deb332476a%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639145225738277333%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=349whvwnOL6s%2BX0RZqbNx%2Bg85tHT2RPMgrC8YpsmPEc%3D&reserved=0>  told the University of Pennsylvania class of 2004, “and it’s waiting for you to hammer it into shape.” I want to believe in this kind of rallying cry, but the lack of specificity in such mass encouragement can make it feel a little toothless. (Is the world waiting as eagerly for the guy who spent all second semester dozing through econ to hammer?)

The best graduation speeches, I think, are the ones grounded in personal experience, the ones that ring not only sincere, but also profoundly felt. You may not be a Taylor Swift <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fa%2F7c_jm7IQWtglo63WFNoYvQ~~%2FAAAAARA~%2FXS-oe1cYtIjsggFu9WHhIQCxYvKThQ5BI1P13VuR8MR_BclX0qdneNUo-hM0T-KWpZpw31VH40RczcB02GUVj7FfdNYoEf0UtJPFDkWoUPZYmK0Y_XG05Zkg69tJ6kFbV3BK1sn9FuaV-Yfkt3Q8_8B8YqRSocO0uCYLqaTb_6x5DHCtZuC7K3hTKiT8Vupc7naRtrKBMkFJ8tc8mG7d4xPNmp0NoNsKw5mW49nPI3n5U7AxTDgv-dwcB0UqCwyAWbJ08YPZ0_IoYj3hd6icfmG8c09Wqa3sRqLYywx0jjgZqy2o3Ue6nV2b7zdM3ravsx-UeDssZdzGlWtb8coCbr64hbXx4Xo-b_bkSgciOBam-kXRS_u8jvDBzYvm6LGSpOgZdvA0jc3QHKYKOlNlPfMXGp-15Q7aW4R_w0djsvI~&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cbe58141735e04683031f08deb332476a%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639145225738312918%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=tBgQMwM4R53NYoT5%2BSJY0d5t92pqP5tYJ9hoGl6lkjU%3D&reserved=0>  fan, but you knew she was speaking from her soul when she told N.Y.U.’s 2022 graduates: “Never be ashamed of trying. Effortlessness is a myth.” Yes! Anyone can see that Taylor Swift tries hard, that her success has come via fist-clenching, teeth-gritting effort. “The people who wanted it the least were the ones I wanted to date and be friends with in high school,” she continued. “The people who want it most are the people I now hire to work for my company.” If a billionaire is going to genuinely connect to an audience of debt-saddled grads, she has to show that she came by her wisdom honestly. She has to truly mean it.

In George Saunders’s speech, he tells a story about a girl in his seventh-grade class who was “mostly ignored, occasionally teased,” and how he could tell this hurt her. He wasn’t mean to her, he says, but, 42 years on, he regretted that when he witnessed her suffering he responded “sensibly, reservedly, mildly.” The oft-quoted line is, “What I regret most in my life are failures of kindness,” but the line that I like even better is more direct: “What’s our problem? Why aren’t we kinder?” He goes on to propose some theories, and some solutions. I love this speech because it emerges from a relatable personal experience, and it dwells in specifics rather than conceptual oratory. Every person present has their own failures of kindness. Everyone present is implicated.

The Sontag quote at the top of this newsletter is actually from a graduation speech she gave at Wellesley College in 1983 <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fa%2FldJNbx9n3v82W09f-nZScA~~%2FAAAAARA~%2Fdi1_2nNZti88QrbW_xjFWQ1nHvkZg1MbrY7hSoKPMsNdZqqwcJFNunGcaj94UH1nIOMn48LtmZChAKU3c90gX9roz1GytaNII2WCO8XYNAu6S5on4_Q3we_jXmUYfWNzYRddHnRMR6oixhjIo_xBPS9OCRPdK5FPAd9318He7nQ0xty8XU2_jy9AKcncxpGomMJ76BzHGoxt2DAERHdS7k91Nq5YennsyH1WLwo679EgmA9qBwfrkaXZoxEAm9YQUpBZLDdL82BY5NYxGQxPVXojr4JXRZmfpyXavJBwp5Y36DH0TkHfu8vhd-PvVRdrl9HkCI5AGqw0N4fnKYaRJG5LfBWlhBPEVJCZXsAov70Y__BGLlyv1WyGOEYx4Ul-_8oY8V0Pl20lotrAauKd8Q~~&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cbe58141735e04683031f08deb332476a%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639145225738333004%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=AV8%2FGHSyWuBcNhWUCy8OwJ2RdVWNDE18tvg%2BPHVBir0%3D&reserved=0> . It has one more line that I love, that, if I must receive life advice via Instagram quote card, I would be delighted to see in my feed. She tells the graduates that the most useful suggestion she can make is that they go on being students for the rest of their lives, and then says, “Don’t move to a mental slum.”

I don’t know exactly what that means, to move to a mental slum, but I find her admonition witty and hyperbolic and inarguably wise. And, like the most enduring speeches, it still has impact. Sontag wasn’t optimistic about the world into which her audience was graduating, but she felt it urgent that they not abandon their education when they exited the halls of knowledge. She concludes by telling them if they stop reading or looking at art or “whatever feeds your head now,” then they’re getting old. I think about this a lot — what feeds my head. And her sign-off was appropriately encouraging: “I wish you love. Courage. And fantasy.” I wish that for us, perpetual students all, no matter what we’re commencing this spring.

You made it through the semester, Blue Devils!

The month of May celebrates Asian American and Pacific Islander heritage and is a time to reflect on the perseverance and joy of these groups and individuals. Beginning in the early 2000s, The Asian American Studies Working Group (AASWG) called out the lack of opportunity to study Asian American and Asian culture at Duke, and in turn asked Duke to establish an Asian American studies program. During the time, they were in contact with student organizations at peer universities, who were in the process of establishing their own Asian American studies programs and departments, helping to inform the movement at Duke. AASWG also participated in the nationwide Abercrombie and Fitch protests, calling out the unwillingness of the corporation to recognize the consequences of including racist graphics on their merchandise. Included below are some print materials showcasing the activities of the Asian American Studies Working Group in 2002.

Despite the efforts of the working group, a department of Asian American and Diaspora Studies wasn’t established at Duke until 2018, which today offers a minor in Asian American and Diaspora Studies. Reestablished in 2016, AASWG has been working on expanding the offerings of the department and representation of the Asian and Asian American student experience at Duke as a whole.  They are still active in doing so. It provides a pretty good sense of what was on the agenda, at least for the Americans. Many of Trump’s top guys were up front, including the secretaries of State, Treasury and Defense. Xi shook hands with all of them, including the China hawks.

In the next rows were the titans of industry, many with business in and with China. There was the leader of Cargill, the agricultural behemoth that wants China to start buying U.S. soybeans, sorghum and beef again. Elon Musk of Tesla and SpaceX was there, along with Tim Cook of Apple, David Solomon of Goldman Sachs and others. The chief executive of Boeing joined them. During the summit, Trump announced China had made a big order of jets <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fnewsletter%2F2o5JT3tbbJDwa5f3OHSR0A~~%2FAAAAARA~%2F0eGHxCYCeUbXFnB0aYxdazi-klMebIWUlLkQL7l9D0OF6gfQa1FyrlysnJMngSh87WemiUKxBYa_yYlDy6YGMDMu1D8v2aEUkPcV5cikqXHJEhf2fBDdcWNWOqVNQ4dYE8QRsjCvw0YPhfzBg3Oy3A3fyHIBNr9FaD4jLvZgiIuRJuVkuoPFSJgtzmhw_B2JhOxI3KbgX67pJuFxcOQmfeL2i8vsq4QMgg2ffhyht2f4tjtRfHNHd3pNxVam-lfJHX4iOerx8BkNFRdUd-Prwn3_4jEX53GvGEuj1qg5DV2C9rEu3QJkL9I2gZu8HXLxl8YfAT2itATfCmPf0pOyv_P2sL93vXTy20d6jRwklPYIw0GXbWgHaNu3JCxjFSD8oYgRXVeZ_dWoOINOphYiRw~~&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cd93088be620b40f8552d08deb26f2ee1%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639144387819077906%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=39KNEJ7QhRLhSJge%2F2RrRDfyizyNzM0uXhcz9twoa%2Bg%3D&reserved=0>  from the company. China was silent.

But if Trump wanted trade out of the summit, Xi’s agenda was focused on Taiwan. At a dinner served at ornate, gold-plated settings (read about the menu <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fnewsletter%2FyiwZHVWna6iLIGf15KuA-w~~%2FAAAAARA~%2FvIoDf556xAwGAnHFHcy3SVvIO7Qakc-PplxufHYPZz1w66PBqwlqpzx3c-a6L-csp58-pAin-rzg0pXZGkXjX6kISWe7-jCEtBg_4mQKA9WHzBl-l7ec3RhUuJyUblFRGlRY5LwZHwOOcceSQfdSFOGkEqkLaL7RHP2WPjIdbdvgYRKO8ryDR6ZPSMHznjttpzLR_DPN0CQzCXgQ7Gagu_--fcsf8KIBY1MC0PpVvRHyPCJPSzpt3mFJwBp3Fvx2Hx3pNAh7lq-91wDZr-N1NzyQer2_-AX5BVup5bJA67RYqbi9dgLNG4oIr5XRpWJU6IWMLuCgTyax3FqlI_neVUfIc6-ayYdaMyqKMejg-snr3Fk2rX9TpybrD4M4_RQK&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cd93088be620b40f8552d08deb26f2ee1%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639144387819105877%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=uFQApLkRH6Ui7zy5cPDEJtn46CHIMxELJHdjios02ZY%3D&reserved=0> ), Xi said that China and America can both be made great again, together. But after journalists left the room, my colleague Chris Buckley reported <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fnewsletter%2FpqA4dBDyD97yw0W9SiaV3g~~%2FAAAAARA~%2FWNX0fGN4igzTcxDZrVnHNF1p1efUolBPogAAJar2JTYrP_nzuYgJ5hk1JL9q4zPMToNYJ0Qbp0b5Re-NKp0-GPVnXTLpVgKbdfRFuk7P_V_CeLWM35rdcJURiya14UqXUcmXVyvHiTPMT35XURY3c7IyD2vtGgo-K21hw50iK-8h12ST-woERiwIJG2tEKFhUKrKmM4QDnJc18PYxUUr0ZCk2bY5F0yjjN4xmWfZLnx1kjBAi99AB7WMuFb4m9fE6iQgDO2ymTvWkTO62kSslHkvdB2H0htLzi8dP4FuqNxByK9zhGRkdUwD2HYuQ3yvCXNDe8yM_7d0gdRfFeph-homubXEQ7BXqh7Za0sRoXZQuMoDvrGt0MQ9RNRyzjS3&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cd93088be620b40f8552d08deb26f2ee1%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639144387819119099%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=ldvvybobihTUxIPzOCLjYgJ%2FN808POotDkV%2FB0uSmpg%3D&reserved=0> , Xi gave a blunt warning about Taiwan: “If handled poorly, the two countries will collide or even clash, putting the entire U.S.-China relationship in an extremely dangerous situation.”

Xi cited the “Thucydides Trap,” the idea that conflict is inevitable <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fnewsletter%2FF83HxM0axa_StSZp7oYPmw~~%2FAAAAARA~%2FUdPuB0hI6Rls0kgltxX3wbsXk9wjmGCexSPsGw8U25SUW75kisqKoBmoAPkqksLa21KGWQMUlqXnGhwZPlc1xyDEI5AN4b9zyKikGY12gwzKPDslO4ebdCFDoDvUPW7YBawM06S1tRPEY6mj9fxt961OlsD57O5R-UQXFZWkvBTYrDe41N9zXdLsqrSl66VyK_OZ8XGVxHr4QAzErjtb5ksL3Vg8WtQ-XZFKdlaexHxuXQGNNXXTOF9sZE6VW1Y1UOePiGFfeGOTY9uK7q68nmEkvVoRJ9CvKN5EWincPogdI3saJZm-NjRJbQWsu9i8ICOo6Ta-sYAKHUKd-C_q-9wzj36aAIc9lRcfC1G3MCOdc-IdQMTHmmY9fjovEH5dKlL5ExBcr009Y1TwlHo2eXKp7-GzNz4k4ThzSUreEwA~&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cd93088be620b40f8552d08deb26f2ee1%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639144387819132758%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=uHYfJpgFhoqs0NXOawjvrTO%2FPXd2I2qV9YR01n%2BwxaA%3D&reserved=0>  when a rising power faces an incumbent one. He said the United States and China could avoid clashing if they both pursued stability — a word rarely associated with Trump.
Another photograph, by Kenny Holston, captured the attention of Joe Kahn, our executive editor, who won a Pulitzer Prize for his reporting on China. I asked Joe to tell us what he saw in the image:

A day of stagecraft and ceremony. Xi receives Trump with his feet firmly planted on the red carpet, arm raised high in preparation for a handshake. Trump approaches with his arm held low and his palm open.
Both of these leaders choreograph meetings obsessively. So this is a moment. The American leader appearing deferential as China’s leader welcomes him from a position of strength.

She found a mixture of anger and amusement, and a sense that the United States is to blame for their slowing economy and rising fuel prices. Some highlights:
In Beijing: “Trump is the kind of person who says one thing today and another tomorrow when he gets back to the United States,” an investor told her. “His words can actually stir up things globally.”

In Fuzhou: “He’s not friendly to China,” a nail salon worker said. Tariffs and the U.S.-China trade war had dampened earnings for her customers. “I think at his age, he doesn’t need to be president anymore.”

In Jinan: One cabdriver thought it was significant that Trump would visit to bend Xi’s ear. “It means that this trade war isn’t just unsuccessful for China, it means that the U.S. is also struggling,” he said.

column1: Can you give some tips for distinguishing between real and fake content (A.I., conspiracy theories, misquotes, etc.)? This used to be relatively simple but seems to get harder by the day. How can we stay informed and accurate? | Sophie O’Driscoll | Copenhagen, Denmark
Steven Lee Myers, who covers the spread of information, replies:

You’re right. It’s getting harder. The social media giants have largely abandoned the fight against fake content, even as technology has made it easier to create and spread it. Some companies offer tools to detect videos made with A.I., but they’re not always definitive — and they’re not convenient to use as you scroll through your feed. Organizations like FactCheck.org and PolitiFact do a great job calling out politicians’ lies or conspiracy theories. In Europe, the European Union maintains a database of Russian disinformation. Unfortunately, there’s no silver bullet. The best advice still is to consider the source. Chances are “some random guy on the internet” is less reliable than a government agency or a news organization.

Learn more below about the Fulbright awards* for undergraduate seniors and recent graduates, graduate students, experienced scholars, and professionals at all career levels.

The Fulbright Awards are some of the most well-known, and thus, some of the most competitive in the world. Fulbright applications require a Personal Statement and Statement of Grant Purpose (a research, study or teaching proposal). Also, most applicants need to identify a host institution abroad and gather recommendation letters, among other elements. It's an intense application process that offers an incredible international exchange opportunity to those who approach the application with purpose.
In this 3 hour workshop, you will learn:

column2: The Fulbright applicant’s formula for success: What to know before you begin
Your Fulbright application plan: Choosing a country and award, planning your application activities & accelerating your productivity
How to do investigative background research on your Fulbright award (and why you shouldn’t miss this step)
Statement of Grant Purpose brainstorming session: How to make your proposal feasible, memorable, and urgent
How to secure not a good – but a *great* – affiliation abroad and how your affiliation impacts your application
The 3 things you must address in your Fulbright Personal Statement and exercises to get you started on your story
How to receive glowing & detailed recommendation letters (even from people who have not seen you in years)
3 secrets to taking your Fulbright application above and beyond

And we have more news below, including a dispatch from a Dutch town hoping for a surge in musketeer tourism. Before we get to it, though: Who’s running in 2028?

The next presidential election is more than two years away. But watch in the coming weeks and months when politicians from out of state start showing up in Iowa to give speeches and shake hands. Online and in the circles I travel in, it’ll lead to a knowing smirk: He’s runnin’. Or she is. Folks in the political class are beginning to think about the future, and about how brightly it could shine on them.

Reid Epstein, who has covered every presidential campaign since 2008, has kept an eye on the shadow campaigns. He maintains a spreadsheet of every potential candidate for the nation’s top job. And today he’s launched it into the world, a very long list of who might run for president in 2028 <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fnewsletter%2FuzfslurJEip5sg7WCp_E6Q~~%2FAAAAARA~%2FhqRPySQlEJZ7-jbcvfZOwoEHOnYGFA0VhRszIUE9uNRgt0KMcla4VldzNDcT79b-sdroRT8106TwlYbm9PsnfUWWxg0KA4F3He-XGF6uLysPl257vUcrSRXXsgILXjxU9uIf0GP8IBK57kJuvttJn9EJevNH0O6bfLCPPMJU5QTj4B_hRHqEthPzaQwirPsBuRLvoR1gqsMrbmFZypYkQPydZcwpVQt5joIKoISAggu1KKYS8Vk1F9jF0GTByb-APtVEuCbRc0-Rry2apx1zrb2fbpVEEpQjcjqtD_8pxXMDhkNBuW5xDQWUX1J1W-9iXc5K3C6ESB5cCVInj9Po1we_AmE_yNtGoM91wLNONbTaenv_pVE_as-28u7yFqio&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C31829dabfe9a46bef13508deb1a58a9d%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639143521772173254%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=5UeXVSPTDp0VWALMhgJPHZN4UV3pWAOHbKUB0oyR7xY%3D&reserved=0> . (He’ll keep it updated as the months spool along, so it’s worth bookmarking.)

Vice President JD Vance isn’t saying much about 2028 right now. His boss is still running the show, and it wouldn’t look good. But he’s styled himself as Trump’s heir for years, and was in Iowa at the start of the month.

Then there’s former Vice President Kamala Harris, who probably has the biggest name in the field. That cuts both ways. Many Democrats may hunger for a candidate less tied to President Joe Biden after their disaster with him in 2024.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio is also in the mix, Vance’s top primary competitor should they both run (or top ally should they run together). He ran for president in 2016.

Other cabinet members have already taken runs at the White House, including Doug Burgum, the interior secretary; Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the health and human services secretary (he ran as both a Democrat and an independent in 2024); and Tulsi Gabbard, the director of national intelligence. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has not made a bid for the presidency before, but now that a lot of people know his name, he might want to try.

Pete Buttigieg, the former transportation secretary, has positioned himself as a possible-future-president ever since he ran in 2020. Rahm Emanuel, the former mayor of Chicago, who was an ambassador, has been putting out a lot of policy proposals — and visiting Iowa, too. Gina Raimondo, the former commerce secretary, appeals to donors but is not well known. Mitch Landrieu, the former New Orleans mayor, who served in the Biden White House? He’s said he may run, as well.
A lot of state leaders, of both parties, would like to make the jump to the national stage.

Among the Democrats, there’s Gavin Newsom of California, one of the loudest anti-Trump voices. Also the billionaire JB Pritzker of Illinois and Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania. And Wes Moore of Maryland has been steadily building a national profile. For the Republicans, it’s possible that Ron DeSantis of Florida could enter the race again. And Greg Abbott of Texas might try for the first time, hopeful that his anti-immigration policies echo nationally. You could see Brian Kemp of Georgia on the hustings, too, along with Sarah Huckabee Sanders of Arkansas and Glenn Youngkin, the former governor of Virginia.

Among the Democrats, there are a lot of possibilities. One is Cory Booker of New Jersey, who ran in 2020. Of course, so did Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota (she’s running for governor this year). Mark Kelly of Arizona has national ambitions. And Chris Van Hollen of Maryland has already traveled to Iowa.
For the Republicans, look to Ted Cruz of Texas and Rand Paul of Kentucky. They both ran in 2016. And to Tim Scott of South Carolina, who ran in 2024.

You’ve got progressive House Democrats like Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York and exiles from Trumpville like Marjorie Taylor Greene. Might Tucker Carlson run for president? Or the sports personality Stephen A. Smith? Donald Trump Jr.? It’s possible!

These are just highlights — there are many more hopefuls in Reid’s catalog. Speaking of politics, Jack Schlossberg, the grandson of John F. Kennedy, holds a narrow lead in a crowded primary for a House seat in New York City. Nicholas Fandos, who’s covering the race, took a close look at Schlossberg’s campaign. Here’s his description of its very first hours:

Aides teed up calls with frenzied media outlets, Democratic luminaries and a roster of wealthy donors. The goal was to show that Mr. Schlossberg, a 33-year-old heir known for his good looks and madcap social media musings, was a serious candidate ready for what promised to be a grueling race.

But just hours into his Day 1 launch, the candidate abruptly announced a change of plans, according to three people familiar with the events. Forget dialing for dollars — Mr. Schlossberg said he needed a nap. He then effectively disappeared for the day, leaving his team reeling.

More erratic behavior and a lot of staff turnover followed. This error occurred because a message was sent to an email address hosted by Office 365, but the address doesn't exist in the receiving organization's Office 365 directory. Directory Based Edge Blocking (DBEB) is enabled for limbcareonline.com, and DBEB rejects messages addressed to recipients who don't exist in the receiving organization's Office 365 directory. This error is reported by the recipient domain's email server, but most often it can be fixed by the person who sent the message. If the steps in the How to Fix It section above don't fix the problem, and you're the email admin for the recipient, try one or more of the following:
Check that the email address exists and is correct - Confirm that the recipient address exists in your Office 365 directory, is correct, and is accepting messages.
Synchronize your directories - Make sure directory synchronization is working correctly, and that the recipient's email address exists in both Office 365 and in your on-premises directory.

Check for errant forwarding rules - Check for forwarding rules for the original recipient that might be trying to forward the message to an invalid address. Forwarding can be set up by an admin via mail flow rules or mailbox forwarding address settings, or by the recipient via the Forwarding or Inbox Rules features.

Make sure the recipient has a valid license - Make sure the recipient has an Office 365 license assigned to them. The recipient's email admin can use the Office 365 admin center to assign a license to them (Users > Active Users > Select the recipient > Assigned License > Edit).

Make sure that mail flow settings and MX records are correct - Misconfigured mail flow or MX record settings can cause this error. Check your Office 365 mail flow settings to make sure your domain and any mail flow connectors are set up correctly. Also, work with your domain registrar to make sure the MX records for your domain are set up correctly.
For more information and additional tips to fix this issue, see this article <https://go.microsoft.com/fwlink/?LinkId=532972> .

This error occurs because the sender sent a message to an email address hosted by Office 365 but the address is incorrect or doesn't exist at the destination domain. The error is reported by the recipient domain's email server, but most often it must be fixed by the person who sent the message. If the steps in the How to Fix It section above don't fix the problem, and you're the email admin for the recipient, try one or more of the following:
The email address exists and is correct - Confirm that the recipient address exists, is correct, and is accepting messages.

Synchronize your directories - If you have a hybrid environment and are using directory synchronization make sure the recipient's email address is synced correctly in both Office 365 and in your on-premises directory.

Errant forwarding rule - Check for forwarding rules that aren't behaving as expected. Forwarding can be set up by an admin via mail flow rules or mailbox forwarding address settings, or by the recipient via the Inbox Rules feature.

Recipient has a valid license - Make sure the recipient has an Office 365 license assigned to them. The recipient's email admin can use the Office 365 admin center to assign a license (Users > Active Users > select the recipient > Assigned License > Edit).

Mail flow settings and MX records are not correct - Misconfigured mail flow or MX record settings can cause this error. Check your Office 365 mail flow settings to make sure your domain and any mail flow connectors are set up correctly. Also, work with your domain registrar to make sure the MX records for your domain are configured correctly.

The digital world is entering a phase where connectivity is no longer simply an enabler. It is becoming the system itself. Infrastructure, communication, and security technologies are converging into integrated environments designed for continuous, real-time operation. Developments in April 2026 reflect a clear shift toward building a connected world where systems are expected to operate seamlessly across physical and digital boundaries.

This shift is being shaped by several significant developments. Amazon.com, Inc. announced a definitive merger agreement to acquire Globalstar, Inc., enabling Amazon Leo to incorporate direct-to-device services into its low-earth-orbit satellite network. This allows smartphones to connect directly to satellites, extending cellular coverage beyond terrestrial limitations.

By integrating Globalstar’s spectrum and proven mobile satellite services capabilities with the scale and reach of Amazon Leo, the company is positioning itself to deliver continuous connectivity across consumer, enterprise, and government use cases worldwide. At the same time, Stellantis entered a five-year strategic partnership with Microsoft to accelerate its digital transformation. The collaboration focuses on building an AI-powered ecosystem that enhances engineering capabilities while embedding cybersecurity directly into vehicle architecture.

Data across mobile applications, in vehicle systems, and cloud environments is secured as part of the system itself. In parallel, Zyxel Networks introduced the WBE665S, a BE22000 12 stream WiFi 7 Triple Radio NebulaFlex Pro ruggedized access point. Designed for professional installers operating in harsh environments such as manufacturing plants, cold storage facilities, and warehouses, the system combines high-capacity performance with an IP67 rated weatherproof design and intelligent cloud management.

Together, these developments point to a broader shift toward communication-centric infrastructure and a more connected world. Connectivity is no longer defined by speed alone. It is becoming foundational to how systems operate, scale, and interact. At the same time, cybersecurity is evolving into both a product feature and a regulatory necessity, particularly in the automotive industry. Standards such as UNECE WP.29 now require manufacturers to implement risk management and software update governance systems, embedding security directly into system design.

Demand signals reinforce this transition. According to the Cisco State of Wireless Report, WiFi has developed into a multiplier effect producing strategic growth engine. Nearly three out of five businesses are planning to implement WiFi 7 in the coming years, driven by the expansion of AI workloads, the Internet of Things, and high-bandwidth applications such as augmented reality, virtual reality, and 4K and 8K streaming. As a result, wireless modernization is becoming central to digital infrastructure strategies.

Several trends are accelerating this shift. AI-powered cybersecurity platforms are becoming essential as systems expand and threats increase in sophistication. Multi-band satellite architecture is improving reliability and performance by combining frequency bands such as C, L, Ka, Ku, and V. Direct-to-device connectivity is reducing reliance on terrestrial networks and expanding access to remote regions. At the same time, advancements in WiFi 7 are enabling low latency and ultra-fast connectivity, supporting remote work, streaming, and smart home ecosystems.

From a market perspective, the impact is already visible. Cybersecurity is becoming a mandatory layer in modern vehicle architecture, while also enabling new revenue streams. Growth in the connectivity market is being fueled by industrial IoT, immersive media, and high-bandwidth applications. At the same time, the industry is shifting from hardware-based models toward software-driven platforms, supported by regulation-driven expansion and the need for integrated solutions.

However, scaling this infrastructure introduces several challenges. Cybersecurity risks remain a major concern, with increasing remote attacks that require no physical proximity to systems. The transition to WiFi 7 requires significant investment in new switches, cabling, and compatible devices, creating capital expenditure challenges for small and medium-sized businesses.

Satellite connectivity also depends on supporting infrastructure such as gateways and integration with terrestrial networks, which can slow adoption. In addition, orbital crowding is emerging as a real risk. In April 2026, a Starlink satellite broke up in orbit, prompting SpaceX to reposition approximately 4,500 satellites to alleviate congestion, highlighting the complexity of managing large-scale satellite networks.

Looking ahead, the next phase will be defined by deployment at scale. AI-driven cybersecurity platforms are expected to move from pilot to implementation, including the expansion of vehicle Security Operations Centers and AI-based anomaly detection across fleets. Stellantis and Microsoft are strengthening global cyber defense capabilities through AI-driven analytics to protect vehicles, customers, and operations worldwide. At the same time, WiFi is entering a new growth phase. WiFi 7 is expanding rapidly and laying the foundation for WiFi 8 and mmWave technologies, enabling deployments that improve user experience, generate income, and lower operational costs. As WiFi converges with 5G and eventually 6G, organizations will be able to build smarter factories, smarter cities, and new ways to involve customers.

Another critical development is the expansion of direct-to-device connectivity. Companies are working to bring satellite-based broadband directly to smartphones. In April 2026, AST SpaceMobile received a commercial license from the Federal Communications Commission to use spectrum from partner mobile network operators such as Verizon, AT&T, and FirstNet. Operating in low-band frequencies between 700 MHz and 800 MHz, this enables seamless space-based cellular broadband for everyday users, helping people stay connected regardless of location.

What is emerging is a digital ecosystem where connectivity, cybersecurity, and infrastructure are tightly integrated to support continuous, real-time operations. The ability to scale will depend on how effectively these elements are combined into systems that are both resilient and adaptable.

This is the moment when automotive cybersecurity, WiFi 7, and satellite internet collectively indicate the rise of next-generation connectivity infrastructure designed for autonomy, scalability, and resilience.

column1: Good morning. I am really looking forward to introducing you to the last full-time museum taxidermist in the United States. But first, a few things.
President Trump and Xi Jinping in Busan, South Korea, last year.  Haiyun Jiang/The New York Times

“This is not how President Trump wanted to arrive in China,” my colleague David Sanger writes <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fnewsletter%2F_uHRI04qh9BJLmevQoajAg~~%2FAAAAARA~%2F-7CluAovpAwHyRZaMn78gDzg7I-QQifcTMFnfXENaT0coZUAOw1jk0-c1zsbywl9EZBkMcVx2G73tTnuzaEprRc6aHnNvkycV4HrQbQNCcOeXHg7CfC8OHNmJSHOJkgo0Xu5f4Nuax8MmiUNDb7KTJQ4Of8R7QjqI4G8oKsN5uPOHa09eYGk8EK5xo5GxwnqUkJm4EvXRtYb9XNiirz-b0kRplD1x88IRi2oGRZR7VpHZgyQ3D0m4fApR8FN7a6mXSKHFXurtW-QSOjcvSFffJljDuntulb7x4o0vWtViDXbUCHfbSeuOImqyqeiS_7rMyT9NzDV7PTy9VnZGAM3wxCPPvxyP2RAiE8YTH0CHqM~&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Ccc73b7804f84428e6bca08deb0dbc817%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639142655187736587%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=XsKmdMz8io57OdnifhmFRJuNWUjKXdHQQ9mfLMvZazA%3D&reserved=0> .

Six weeks ago, Trump pushed off his summit meeting with China’s leader, Xi Jinping, because of the war in Iran. He’d thought the conflict would be over by now, showing Beijing that reports of America’s demise as a superpower were premature. Instead, David writes, Trump starts the meeting today “bogged down by a far lesser power in a war he started.”

But Xi’s in a tough spot, too. China gets more than 30 percent of its oil from the Persian Gulf, which is now cut off. Economic growth there is falling as energy prices rise. “The result is that this is a summit like few others,” David writes. It features the world’s two dominant superpowers looking hobbled. Experts aren’t optimistic the sides will announce a major economic deal or resolve their differences.

Smaller nations across Asia are worried about that, my colleague Damien Cave reports <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fnewsletter%2FxlBHPBi9LqJT5Wn5X6m7FQ~~%2FAAAAARA~%2FO-e3gevtRvgb8JBhHh5q2M73UpIqHMLQDY7Zmaz9BxUs18bHeIRSCgdBSAIuLK-_gxmJh-GwWybNng4ORzwwXcGuEpNkxoY5gJx1DmEsCMuwZPmIJRwdkAMwp5UCTyOucanzj3b_qBnYMMoNBEOJB7NPUwQPaEOf-VFtBvk2DKV0roPewBdKMZjM-M7Soy4sPoRSBOvWDCocxZwyyxzkOL8IvkW-VTOUWBOGTrew1m4-nJRirMZ4VDSqZFnE9_0ruuSz4kxr5Oql2mZxAIWg1fxcd18wqATC0VsV8uNbhPwkEFklez9aziaLXiaEyQ4V9m3sOFNtNTDCNRRw3BAhZwu2ZAivh27EI6Y55_QKWqOHcuiSHyfsHH8TR3ci5Wu1&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Ccc73b7804f84428e6bca08deb0dbc817%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639142655187759590%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=Y2sGEXJbIOXv7IsC92tuE2HHdVJDSSRdi%2BNwS1jvN%2F4%3D&reserved=0> . As the summit looms, they’re “behaving as if they are stuck in ‘Godzilla’ or ‘Dune’ — moving quietly in small groups, trying not to provoke the wrath of petulant giants.”
Here’s some of what Trump and Xi may discuss:

Trade: Trump hopes China will buy lots of American soybeans, beef and Boeing airplanes. Xi is likely to push for an extension of last year’s trade truce between the U.S. and China, and for the right to import more A.I. computer chips.

Taiwan: Currently, the U.S. says it “does not support” Taiwanese independence. China wants Trump to actively oppose it — and to stop selling Taiwan weapons. (That’s unlikely. But it’s Trump. He could always go off script.)

Iran: Trump will ask Xi to persuade Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Xi’s administration has prodded Iranian officials to negotiate with the U.S., but Beijing sees the war as Washington’s problem.
How badly has China been hit by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz? — Cameron Tran, United States

Despite being the largest importer of crude oil through the Strait of Hormuz, China has weathered the crisis relatively well. It has been stockpiling oil since last year. China is estimated to have about four months of imports saved up. The country has also aggressively invested in renewable energy and boasts the largest fleet of electric vehicles in the world. China’s demand for fossil fuels fell over the past two years. Still, China has felt some of the war’s effects. Restaurants and hotels report fewer guests. Car sales plunged in April.

Almost everywhere in the country, students’ academic performance is worse than their peers’ was a decade ago, according to district-level test score data that came out this morning <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fnewsletter%2FaKINJ8DJ3StniTOVbQLP-w~~%2FAAAAARA~%2FqsS0fZVVyP8Z-fy5yhMqMsLcQnZmaLBxs5NqY7F3VNdYE1bXPyx2oz-MyWFapq8VjRLNhN3mpTrTiiUZkDEaiyb0iE3BTKLLaM36XZr98wwGK1uv8RiZbFlQz1cAoPHw22l_POLccS2HKPeOpWSd-eYeYOW5F2yGFD1qDGDueoTdnAsVVzN5QR6G-FRYmmkwU-GNjl5GAf2vnClxXR10rQpVl-VDKkghQdgq9GQ1nRi___xSaC2e-48hqXAaJOhPN5u-aioS9B13LjCOaYh1o8sijv-dSIP36rSOFRPB__of6nKtg48-seTRPW3AlYhBCOs9iwMwJ4u465ZeiQZ3a3cgGNlmE_yVPwGosifyoT0EYn_x71Wc0oqDtNwBveWi&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Ccc73b7804f84428e6bca08deb0dbc817%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639142655187912660%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=4mopIxqAUfEALVEbgkWiXVRkedvLqKIYBN0XWDZqWfA%3D&reserved=0> .
The numbers are startling. Reading scores were down last year in 83 percent of school districts for which we have data. Math scores were down in 70 percent.

The drops happened in rich districts as well as poor ones — in urban, suburban and rural ones. They crossed racial divides. And the biggest losses of all were among the lowest-achieving kids. In one in three school districts in the U.S., my colleagues report, students are reading a full grade level lower than they were in 2015.

Education experts told The Times that there’s no single reason for this learning recession. But federal school accountability has relaxed since the No Child Left Behind Act was replaced in 2015. There was also the rise of iPhones, social media and school-issued laptops. And of course the pandemic didn’t help. Student absenteeism spiked and remains high in its wake.

column1: Streaming, Toilet Paper, Underwear: Subscription Fatigue Is Setting In
As companies look to build cash flow and loyalty, everything from heated car seats to earthworm deliveries can become a recurring charge on your credit card.
The first law that needs to be passed is one that requires subscriptions to be as easy to cancel as they are to start.
Companies that allow subscriptions to be created online but don’t allow cancellation online are thieves.

At a larger level, this is part of the ""Right to Repair"" movement that has been proposed. Things you don't own, you often cannot fix - a new form of planned obsolescence. You're locked into using the services of the original manufacturer.

Tim Bovard, the last full-time taxidermist at any museum in the United States, has been working at the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County since 1984. column1: Don’t say you weren’t warned. Repeatedly.

Michael Burry, the fund manager played by Christian Bale in “The Big Short,” compared recent, frenetic tech-stock action to the “scene of the bloody car crash, minutes before it happens” in a Substack post <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45688997.406455%2FaHR0cHM6Ly9zdWJzdGFjay5jb20vaG9tZS9wb3N0L3AtMTk3MTc2ODUyP21vZD1kamVtTWFya2V0c0FN%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dB255fd780&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cd2f35582a8a94b26bd8308deb0dbb873%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639142654928044916%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=9pC6FSXawGRE8bHeqjS3NLBQ8RL2qFnaOvt6WUi2%2B3c%3D&reserved=0>  this week. He recommended selling stocks in the market’s hottest corners.

Burry goes by the moniker “Cassandra Unchained <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45688997.406455%2FaHR0cHM6Ly94LmNvbS9taWNoYWVsamJ1cnJ5P21vZD1kamVtTWFya2V0c0FN%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dBf220a9da&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cd2f35582a8a94b26bd8308deb0dbb873%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639142654928086706%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=rsipFv6dup6xGkH4uI9bewaij3RJZwonHOTEdvzEeKs%3D&reserved=0> ” on social media. Since the epic housing bet that made him famous, though, he’s been the inverse of that mythological princess. She was cursed with seeing the future but not being believed.

Burry, whose firm didn’t respond to emails, has received lots of media attention <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45688997.406455%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cud3NqLmNvbS9maW5hbmNlL3N0b2Nrcy9taWNoYWVsLWJ1cnJ5LWJldHMtaGUtaXNudC10b28tZWFybHktdG8tZ28tYWdhaW5zdC10aGUtYWktanVnZ2VybmF1dC01ZDk1ZDIxZT9tb2Q9ZGplbU1hcmtldHNBTQ%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dB797484ab&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cd2f35582a8a94b26bd8308deb0dbb873%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639142654928105895%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=yE4ccAyFsA%2BnO57kUcCjh5jl49AH4y7kG%2BbrFQH6zpY%3D&reserved=0>  for his often-cryptic warnings. He famously tweeted “SELL” in January 2023 before deleting his X account. In 2022, he wondered whether an economic downturn could be “worse than 2008.” And he warned about a “bubble” in passive investing in September 2019.

Even for those not managing money, the financial and emotional rewards from predicting a calamity are large. Consider Roger Babson, who got rich off of investing newsletters in the 1920s and 1930s. What Chapter Am I Closing? (A May Reflection for Graduates and Career Transitioners)
May is graduation season—a time when thousands of people are closing one chapter and beginning another. But transitions aren't just for new graduates walking across a stage in a cap and gown.

Maybe you're finishing a degree. Maybe you're leaving a job. Maybe you've been in the same role for years and you're ready for something different. Maybe you just got rejected from an opportunity you wanted and now you're being forced into a transition you didn't choose.
Before you rush into the next thing, take time to reflect on what you're actually closing and what you want to begin.
Pull out your journal and reflect on these questions:
Part 1: What Chapter Am I Closing?

column2: What role, identity, or phase of life am I leaving behind right now? (Be specific—""college student,"" ""marketing associate,"" ""person who's been trying to break into consulting for 3 years,"" etc.)
What did this chapter teach me? What skills, relationships, or insights am I taking with me?
What am I ready to leave behind from this chapter? (Toxic work culture? Trying to impress people who don't matter? Saying yes to everything? A field that doesn't align with my mission?)
What will I miss about this chapter, even if I'm ready to move on?

column1: Part 2: What Chapter Am I Beginning?

column2: What do I want my next chapter to be about? (Not just a job title—what do I want to be learning, building, or contributing?)
What does success look like in this next chapter?
What scares me most about this transition? (Be honest—fear of failure, financial instability, starting over, being behind peers, making the wrong choice?)
If I trusted myself completely, what would my next bold move be?

column1: Part 3: How Do I Navigate the In-Between?

column2: While I'm in transition, what do I need to protect? (My mental health? My financial stability? Time to think strategically rather than react?)
What story am I telling myself about this transition—and is it helping or hurting me? (""I'm behind"" vs. ""I'm being strategic."" ""I failed"" vs. ""I'm pivoting."")
What's one action I can take this week to move toward my next chapter, even if I don't have all the answers yet?
