column1: They were hip, rich and wore really comfortable shoes. What could go wrong?

Allbirds wasn’t just the unofficial footwear provider <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45066239.467906%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cud3NqLmNvbS9zdHlsZS9mYXNoaW9uL2hvdy1hbGxiaXJkcy1iZWNhbWUtc2lsaWNvbi12YWxsZXlzLWZhdm9yaXRlLXNuZWFrZXItMTE2MDUwNDMxNDk_bW9kPWRqZW1NYXJrZXRzQU0%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dBba83c5a9&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C51c3f5da062a47ae9c4c08de93ca8ee2%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639110695366536107%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=7tTxSF1gJDtC%2BFV9RV2hdmX8D1fF%2F0I9j0g1nAETJzk%3D&reserved=0>  of Silicon Valley—its initial public offering in 2021 tapped into the tech sector’s ethos by giving the company’s founders disproportionate sway in how it would be run.

Now that they’ve run it into the ground <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45066239.467906%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cud3NqLmNvbS9idXNpbmVzcy9yZXRhaWwvYWxsYmlyZHMtdGhlLXRlY2gtYnJvLWZhdm9yaXRlLW9uY2UtdmFsdWVkLWF0LTQtYmlsbGlvbi1qdXN0LXNvbGQtaXRzLWFzc2V0cy1mb3ItbmV4dC10by1ub3RoaW5nLTYwNWUzMjE2P21vZD1kamVtTWFya2V0c0FN%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dBb5defe28&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C51c3f5da062a47ae9c4c08de93ca8ee2%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639110695366550901%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=vFms1mRdUim1oisUc%2FTu83u4CWPCLPZBpBnn%2BlNuGwE%3D&reserved=0> , some investors are blaming dual-class voting structures for its and similar stocks’ woes. Maybe executives’ missteps could have been avoided with the discipline of outside pressure?

Salad chain Sweetgreen, eyewear seller Warby Parker, language-learning app Duolingo and social network Snap all have share classes with extra votes for founders and each has incinerated billions in shareholder wealth recently.

They’re an easier sell when the investing public is optimistic. Supervoting shares became especially popular for tech IPOs during bubbly 2021. The structure had a revival last year with companies like Klarna, Figma and StubHub.

Dual-class shares aren’t new, though, and some have worked out very well. Examples of successful companies that limit outsiders’ sway include Google parent Alphabet, Meta, Dillard’s, Workday, Comcast and, most-famously, Berkshire Hathaway.

“It does seem like, in some ways, having a control situation like that can empower the leader and the company” says Paul Nary, a strategy professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania.

About 10% of all IPOs since 1980 have used a dual-class structure, according to University of Florida Professor Jay Ritter. His database <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45066239.467906%2FaHR0cHM6Ly9zaXRlLndhcnJpbmd0b24udWZsLmVkdS9yaXR0ZXIvaXBvLWRhdGEvP21vZD1kamVtTWFya2V0c0FN%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dB67b8f367&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C51c3f5da062a47ae9c4c08de93ca8ee2%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639110695366566246%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=yuy4BCfQrKdVB2im8s95%2BR9RKpuruTJmTID%2FngDbW7I%3D&reserved=0>  shows that their average three-year, buy-and-hold return has been better than for one-share, one-vote offerings.

Sometimes it gets old: A number of established dual-class companies have languished in the past decade under family control, including Tyson Foods, J.M. Smucker, Scholastic and Brown-Forman. Some controlled by James Dolan <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45066239.467906%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cud3NqLmNvbS9maW5hbmNlL2ludmVzdGluZy90aGUta25pY2tzLWFyZS11bmRlcnZhbHVlZC1maXhpbmctdGhhdC13aWxsLWJlLWhhcmRlci10aGFuLXdpbm5pbmctYS1jaGFtcGlvbnNoaXAtZmFiOGVjZGQ_bW9kPWRqZW1NYXJrZXRzQU0%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dB8477b2f0&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C51c3f5da062a47ae9c4c08de93ca8ee2%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639110695366588464%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=kMtxeX7PFPf0k9gMwrDuGNSogP2XVJy4X6CVbDPw4k8%3D&reserved=0> , including AMC Networks, have long been tarred with a “Dolan discount” for that reason.

On the bright side, Nary says that when an activist investor has managed to get influence over family-controlled companies or a professional outsider CEO is brought in, the improvement in the share price tends to be greater.

Some companies have had such strong-willed and influential founders that they could make bold bets without giving themselves extra votes. Imagine if an activist investor had pressured Jeff Bezos to stop sacrificing profits for growth or Steve Jobs to forget taking on the dominant BlackBerry with his iPhone.

That’s why giving insiders power is so appealing: Investors hope that they’re backing the next Bezos, Jobs or Zuckerberg. They almost never are. If things don’t go according to plan these days, activists will swoop in to salvage some value. Sometimes Wall Street is shortsighted.
Handing company leaders enough rope to hang themselves with occasionally works out.

APPLY! SSMU Project Director and Manager Applications Open," <https://duke.campusgroups.com/read/b659729f-3171-11f1-bd1c-025c6e3d0caf.png> Hi Everyone,
We hope you're doing well! As we begin preparing for the upcoming school year, SSMU is excited to organize SSMU Projects for 2026-2027, as mentioned at our last GBM!

If you haven't heard, SSMU Projects will consist of team-based, semester- or year-long statistical consulting / pro bono data projects that connect undergraduate students with external organizations to apply statistical methods to real-world problems. Each project will be led by experienced student project managers and supported by analysts, focusing on developing practical insights through data analysis and collaboration. This program is designed to provide members with hands-on experience to deepen their statistical/data science experience, build meaningful project work, and engage more actively with SSMU beyond GBMs and with local organizations and external companies.

We are now taking applications for the Project Director and Project Manger roles! Apply here <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fduke.campusgroups.com%2Fclick%3Femail_links_id%3D481235%26member_id%3D26277677&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cec942d453ee848b79ece08de93d852e4%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639110754476170258%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=6jPLvEHvFq6weaQSS0GV2hDyFcwjnBkl%2BX%2BjbOKgyY0%3D&reserved=0>  by April 13th at 11:59 PM!
We received a few questions about Projects that we'd like to discuss:

1. Is there a minimum skill set/qualifications needed to participate?/What level of experience is required for each role? There is no hard requirements. For analysts, we'd recommend STA199 or equivalent. Project managers we expect to have STA221 and/or STA323 experience and maybe some data science experiences. Project Directors should have upper level coursework (STA332 and/or 402 and/or 440) and experience working with real-world data science problems.
2. Are these projects eleigible for course credit? At present time, no.

3. What clients have SSMU reached out to? Since this is a new endeavor, we envision project managers will (with support) reach out to organizations of their choosing. We hope that the projects are broad and reflect the huge variety of applications of statistics.
4. How many hours per week is expected? 5-8 hours per week on average

5. What's the desired scope/direction of projects? This depends on interest. If a majority of analysts have solely STA199 experience, then most projects will be data-science oriented in nature. However, with enough interest from people with STA221 (or greater) experience, more projects can lean towards modeling and more advanced analysis.
Please email ctr22@duke.edu or lm487@duke.edu if you have any additional questions! We're excited for this program and hope you are too!

Alumni Advising with Mark Augusti – open to all undergraduates  REGISTER <https://www.signupgenius.com/go/10C0F44ABAE29A7F5CF8-59754216-finance>
Mondays, 12:00 – 1:00 PM, in the DFE Conference Room (Social Sciences 228A)
Mark Augusti ‘87 holds weekly in-person advising hours for undergrads. This spring, Augusti teaches FMKT 390S-04: Financing Health Care Companies. Read his bio below:

Mark Augusti, MBA, is Founder and Managing Owner of Kenmore Advisors, an advisory and consulting firm focused on compliance, governance, and commercial strategy in the medical technology sector. Previously, Mr. Augusti was President and Chief Executive Officer and a member of the Board of Directors at Conformis, Inc., a public orthopedic device company. Prior to leading Conformis, Mr. Augusti was Integra LifeSciences Corporation’s Corporate Vice President and President of Orthopedics and Tissue Technologies. Mr. Augusti served as Chief Executive Officer at Bioventus LLC, and was a member of the Bioventus’ Board of Directors. Prior to that Mr. Augusti spent nine years with Smith & Nephew, in a series of leadership roles within the orthopedics and biologics businesses. Prior to that, he spent 13 years at GE Medical Systems, where he held various sales, marketing and strategic management roles, both in the U.S. and internationally. Mr. Augusti serves as a director of the Massachusetts Health Policy Forum and has served as a director of the AdvaMed Accel Board. Mr. Augusti received his M.B.A. from the UCLA Anderson School of Management, and his B.S. in Computer Science and Economics from Duke University.

I hope you had a nice weekend!
I am reaching out today to see if you have any other questions before you accept your offer for our Semester 2 2026 (late July to late November) program here at the University of Sydney.

We process acceptances on a rolling basis and the sooner you complete the acceptance of offer process the sooner you can get started with the next steps to come to Australia.  Generally speaking, students coming to Sydney for Semester 2 typically have finalised their acceptance of offer process by early-to-mid May at the latest.

There are several important steps you will need to complete before you can apply for a student visa.  The sooner you complete all of these steps, the more time you will have for your visa application process:

column2: Share a copy of the photo page of your current valid passport – The identity document you provided in your USYD application is a drivers license, which is not sufficient to apply for a visa.  Before I can issue your eCoE, I will need to receive a copy of the photo page from your valid passport that expires after the end of the program, as the eCoE system requires me to input certain details from your passport photo page.
USYD issues your electronic confirmation of enrolment (eCoE) – An electronic confirmation of enrolment (eCoE) is one document required as part of an application for a student visa.

You submit a visa application to the Department of Home Affairs (DHA) – Information to point students in the right direction to start this process will be provided once it is possible to issue their eCoE.

column1: Your acceptance of offer process will be complete after you have responded to your offer, pay the tuition fee, and make the necessary arrangements for your OSHC policy.  Once this happens I can issue your electronic confirmation of enrolment (eCoE), which is a document you’ll need from me before you can apply for your student visa.

I also wanted to reassure you that here at USYD, students can continue requesting approval for additional units of study from the time of application until the end of the 1st week of classes for the semester.  It’s totally normal that students will usually request a few additional units between application stage and start of classes due to change of mind, updated advice from their home institution, etc.
I look forward to hearing from you soon!
Kristin Johnson | Senior Study Abroad Adviser

column1: As you are planning and preparing for your program, please keep the following key dates for the USYD Semester 2 2026 program in mind:

**It is a requirement of the Duke Study Abroad office that all Duke students arrive to Sydney in time for the start of the official Welcome (Orientation) Week.  For Semester 2 2026, the official Welcome Week begins from Monday morning 27 July which means arriving to Sydney no later than Sunday 26 July.

This means you would need to depart the USA no later than 24 July USA time in order to arrive to Sydney by 26 July Sydney time.

column1: Good morning. We’ll start today behind the moon, farther from Earth than anyone’s ever been.
At 6:44 p.m. Eastern, the crew of NASA’s moon mission Artemis II was cut off from the rest of humanity as the spaceship slipped behind the moon.

For about 40 minutes, no one on Earth could know exactly what the four astronauts were doing. During their interlude in silence, they ventured farther from our planet than anyone who has ever lived. When the spacecraft emerged on the other side, the crew watched as a thin crescent of sunlit Earth rose above the lunar surface.

Since launching to space on Wednesday, the astronauts of Artemis II have relayed observations back to scientists on Earth. They have tangled with the vehicle’s toilet and taken dazzling photos of space. Before their loop around the moon, they also radioed Houston with a request. They asked to name a previously undesignated crater in memory of the wife of Reid Wiseman <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fnewsletter%2FdvKz7cfGpt0Nohp518w4Zw~~%2FAAAAARA~%2FRaVuooirMIqY1qkNeeizlLmEzz_zPY0l26okoFbMp7RuGBTBTDbXe6BIarF6HZ6cJAat0Hmi5EBm45WQhmS5zfVsMeUbs8vHRI8gf4WafiODrbxAOjva9kqZBhxsUl41qtnn1JVBRfbj8ZFEGo8rtydHLa95lFmlMd6Bk5ZitBor_-co__sKIYG_qGjnKpN4rDUyE4Qkd6wQxXU7DY8sCZUeXIJK5FT0Z8eozZ5ije_ambQiloWMeMLs3UQJydrqIv74ajBadWskJ9Tu9ZSsP46Z5HJCu4ZBPveRJ-67LaSaH-4UMKsZcerZbFBb8OfCrxg0etqTAgxrtxa5wKmHv8d6_rNQlrW-wfsZtrY3qIHFuOQSUFC22ODjMa2ypzmlesCPaQKrIqC-ZWIjekcszxpnQPFnuXf_2HpAdfdu4Ps~&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C2891e90662f8417cf9f208de9492c611%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639111555579573839%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=0CrsprzQ3IjX5kKvMU67YNWlfZ5XRA%2Bl53T0phl87fM%3D&reserved=0> , the mission’s commander. She died of cancer in 2020.

“It’s a bright spot on the moon, and we would like to call it Carroll,” said Jeremy Hansen, the mission specialist, his voice breaking up. The astronauts embraced and wiped their eyes. For a moment, mission control went silent.
— That’s how many miles the Artemis II astronauts were from Earth last night. It’s a big number. Our writer Evan Gorelick offers a few points of comparison.

column2: Wiener dogs: If you took 22-inch dachshunds and laid them nose to tail, you’d need a very cooperative pack of almost 728 million dogs to cover the distance. It would be tough: There are only around 900 million dogs, of any breed, in existence.

Walking a dog: If you took one of the dachshunds on a brisk 3-mile-per-hour walk, you’d need to walk for more than 84,000 hours to get there. That translates to nearly 10 years of continuous walking. (If the dog let out a celebratory bark upon arrival, and if sound could travel through space, it would reach Earth around 14 days later.)

Eating hot dogs: You’d need a chain of 2.37 billion Nathan’s Famous hot dogs to cover the distance. If the competitive eater Joey Chestnut shoveled them down at his record-breaking pace of 76 dogs every 10 minutes, he’d need to eat nonstop for almost 594 years to devour the entire chain. (His monstrous meal would top 700 billion calories.)

column1: In Tehran last week. Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

One of the most difficult things to understand about a faraway conflict is its scale — its size relative to our own lived experience. The graphic designer Massimo Vignelli had a line about that. He said that dimensions are physical, but scale is mental. I always took that to mean that scale exists in the imagination, a frame of mind that tells us more than a list of measurements or a roster of numbers.

Take the war in the Middle East. My colleague Martín González Gómez, a graphics editor, wanted to understand its scale. To show it, he took maps of the conflict and laid them over maps of other parts of the world.
Source: ACLED. Martín González Gómez/The New York Times

The total land area of the countries shooting at each other would cover much of the continental United States. In the overlay, you can see that strikes have happened over what amounts to the distance between Florida and Oregon.
Source: Institute for the Study of War with American Enterprise Institute’s Critical Threats Project. Martín González Gómez/The New York Times
Russia invaded Ukraine four years ago, and each side has fought bitterly over narrow tracts of land. Iran is significantly larger than Ukraine and has more than double its population.
Source: International Maritime Organization. Martín González Gómez/The New York Times

Martín laid a map of the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s supply of oil used to run, over a map of New York City. The narrow shipping channels that Iran has under its control are each about the width of a Manhattan neighborhood.

These maps <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fnewsletter%2FCXdRA9FAMrbA-R37-DsdSQ~~%2FAAAAARA~%2F0d1rZKjggp6Kgo4IjxMxgZMnVnwBLLA72sF3kaKCr0H7Duph2d8Tkmx95fLnTKOdhLDoN9RnWumEMU4IVVNIgQ_mAWXz3TvBNojiPNcB1tkimNQVPGZS1enRP-vV-SLr6sEDvhOnEEwdffnvXv654UaFMY9yp3ndTy4Pw4TGobZDZZnUupOqA6nhyYitAh-PEou4rRVsA-GSRzwpgCPhKVgK1EioEUAKL-z6PFbKpYvKMKn9RZ70y3kz0-zF-MuhFrYr50DD4j2GZpThgLdre8G2lfWOcM9GPwwEVAC51edhwCOiSd9wU5GkfkkIodDKLpkFC3qyCrx5UidMNV-nrVGKU7mHWTDTiljt13yhkTOvWt7L-7uVuzxtfbQL6mrAH0fywnxSJsyzHegnIbQmaQ~~&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C2891e90662f8417cf9f208de9492c611%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639111555579620863%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=EiBSpoHhJmO6c3fEHsR6km06OCNJ9nxoXTPOJmMqMj4%3D&reserved=0>  will help give you a sense of perspective.

column1: There’s an old joke about two economists walking down a busy street. One points to a $20 bill lying on the sidewalk. The other one keeps walking since, if it was really there, someone would have picked it up already.

Market efficiency is one of the most important ideas in finance, but investors can take it too literally. It’s possible the stock market’s mild reaction to the war in Iran—the S&P 500 is down by just 3.9%—reflects everything smart people know about the conflict’s economic effects.

Just as the market is prone to overreact, though, it can be surprisingly slow to grasp the gravity of a really major crisis <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45086558.466903%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cud3NqLmNvbS9hcnRpY2xlcy9iZXdhcmUtb2Ytd2FsbC1zdHJlZXRzLWFybWNoYWlyLWVwaWRlbWlvbG9naXN0cy0xMTU4MTQyMjQwMD9tb2Q9ZGplbU1hcmtldHNBTQ%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dB5cb53c62&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C40b7f30610044b03203608de949327ff%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639111556917654465%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=Dazt7dkysQiTWtS1e7efBXED9%2FMH2Rc2cZIqYG1pTpE%3D&reserved=0> . A big reason is psychological: It takes lots of evidence to convince people something unthinkable might be about to happen like major banks collapsing <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45086558.466903%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cud3NqLmNvbS9hcnRpY2xlcy9TQjEyMjE0NTQ5MjA5NzAzNTU0OT9tb2Q9ZGplbU1hcmtldHNBTQ%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dB0265d283&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C40b7f30610044b03203608de949327ff%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639111556917681835%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=xF0dITJyW4IjokosztsG19g4RLsKRPCjaFg8vHmrmGU%3D&reserved=0> , a pandemic <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45086558.466903%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cud3NqLmNvbS9ncmFwaGljcy9tYXJjaC1jaGFuZ2VkLWV2ZXJ5dGhpbmcvP21vZD1kamVtTWFya2V0c0FN%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dB9eeb27f6&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C40b7f30610044b03203608de949327ff%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639111556917709749%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=674eyIqCxACC0UOof8owR%2FsyaPQCLt8A0OsJjXEEy4U%3D&reserved=0>  or actual fuel shortages <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45086558.466903%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cud3NqLmNvbS9maW5hbmNlL2NvbW1vZGl0aWVzLWZ1dHVyZXMvb2lsLWNyaXNpcy1hc2lhLWV1cm9wZS1hZnJpY2EtaXJhbi13YXItZWE4ODNiYTI_bW9kPWRqZW1NYXJrZXRzQU0%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dBb94a821a&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C40b7f30610044b03203608de949327ff%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639111556917749723%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=ilfUAk5IW8HUjFSB6HsPgtCtv%2BSWal%2FUpz9bH9uZV6g%3D&reserved=0> .

Another culprit is our misplaced faith in Wall Street’s small army of well-paid seers. Five weeks seems like long enough for estimates of the damage from an energy shock to seep into analysts’ forecasts, but that isn’t how it works.

Since the start of the conflict, full-year earnings-per-share forecasts for the S&P 500 as a whole have risen slightly, according to bottom-up numbers from FactSet. More specifically, forecasts for 131 companies have risen and those for 103 have dropped. The remainder are either unchanged or barely changed.

The big risers are mostly no-brainers: Most are in the energy, refining or chemical industries. Analysts who didn’t update those numbers would look dumb. Ditto for those seeing the biggest forecast reductions such as airlines and travel-adjacent companies. The rest had recent bad news, like Nike and Campbell’s.

How can 290 companies’ forecasts be unchanged for a fiscal year that had 10 months remaining, for most of them, when the war started? Even if the U.S. is mostly insulated from fuel shortages and travel disruptions, customers and suppliers of America’s multinational companies aren’t.
The explanation is how analysts work. A problem has to be meaningful for management to tweak its guidance near the end of the quarter. The one that ended last week wasn’t affected much.

And the rest of 2026? Many companies have already been in their unofficial “quiet period” for weeks so even subtle messages to the investor community are frowned upon. Fearful of angering executives, most analysts wait for the company to flag problems.

Yet it would stand to reason, for example, that McDonald’s, which has thousands of restaurants directly in countries under fire and thousands more in places starting to experience fuel shortages, would be affected. One might expect an even bigger impact on a company like DoorDash, since gasoline directly affects the cost of food delivery. Yet forecasts for those and other consumer-facing companies such as Mondelez, Chipotle, Starbucks and PepsiCo are unchanged.
More companies than usual will be sending the market a message through their guidance or the tone of their investor calls in coming weeks. Earnings season is going to be interesting.

This is a reminder that the Commitment to Participate is now availabe in the MyGlobalEd portal. Please digitally sign and submit this Commitment to Participate as soon as you have confirmed your participation in a Duke Approved or Petition program. Submitting this lets Duke know your intentions for Fall 2026. You should sign and submit only one Commitment to Participate per term.

column2: If you have not yet applied to the program, do not submit the Commitment to Participate
If you have not yet received an offer of admission from the program, do not submit the Commitment to Participate
Once you sign the Commitment to Participate, any other applications in the Duke system for this term will be withdrawn.

In Beirut yesterday. Diego Ibarra Sanchez for The New York Times

How steady is the cease-fire in the Middle East? Israeli missiles have continued to fall on Lebanon, Iran threatens a military response, and shippers are confused about the status of the Strait of Hormuz. The United States and Iran don’t even agree on what it will take to open peace talks.

Both sides have declared victory in the conflict. The United States has destroyed most of Iran’s navy and reduced its ability to shoot missiles across the region. But President Trump’s other goals remain unrealized <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fnewsletter%2Fq-z86r9-mk9Z9BV3t6lMyQ~~%2FAAAAARA~%2F0ZxIT5UlKXtzR-VCVf7XUTH4OAgs9UfEZgn1iNSBkVJoTrBZ9PFkZJAgE-eTThE2crPMkW-LVRZHFuhqt6IzpmswL0j-A3QDnwPMEvXF8RrV6ZGr8pRp4hdVFdCNLPS_Ye__Fff-fYstJC3OvVVT5n3YhoiwG4CtAS6dAPzKt3vpTGFQ_uTA2TQS4-Aof-cCbyiswE1zo_um-eUfW7k7TvOPvefezHxy_24vivVA72U3Gma7hxe7fJhGwXsP9xWN0tUHjfZ96Jotcq19Gn9LlUljNsZOhB6AhXSH90eEE6dlSKm7QAIXxv_MoGqp1NVTy3BJSw875c_-6gersvibkmHrcqQwKvPLgx71nhyxvog~&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C5805dcf4a40f49d8746608de9623df5a%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639113278008827199%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=oLIjeAalFIlXI179C8QjvyBnnP4v7Gi0v995wFQgGec%3D&reserved=0> . Iran still has uranium to make a bomb someday; it still guides regional militias like Hezbollah; its regime still holds power and crushes dissent.
And Iran, for its part, now has total control of the strait.
White House officials say talks are expected to begin between the two nations on Saturday, brokered by Pakistan. They are likely to be contentious.

Among other things in its 10-point proposal <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fnewsletter%2FyhBE4WfKGevEz2sxBD4G_g~~%2FAAAAARA~%2FkbrX8_6lfjIOXdDWDxk6dOXsI2bjRxf9aecOo6J6Ki58rHudkzpKs_71nelwZVDckJ7Eh0NLkakBGxgneJ1Cc0Nv0qBtbld2Y-SGdvroXzHlzTXKzCP_Kwvg_b39TW9a6cTe59G-HLEwP1CkGzIreIfF8yCPpAdiDivtrlhBOegjAPDJutL0wPWS15ZtDPnH8G9uPlecqRoXOmtpXCc7xxYrEr_3MiQbJpnT7zsRjl7FViZLI5lmmUq_HQPsvd7UicWZA6_pTEaJJFmgRpDINmFWa6m8REY_MSwfoLjsaXg0_q_tPXfV8XZXrVie0bUOGqXSiNNrvlaXascnJBMqmcnZJ0BmPpqrBLlkD5G0EiRC-YARb-RIxbOOa1q3KRgmWD9sQ_GceJIy9quQDPR2zQ~~&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C5805dcf4a40f49d8746608de9623df5a%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639113278008841920%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=2Y%2FPGHgLbi3yLpVyRfUzoOokSXr8B%2ByVfoPJXSvt544%3D&reserved=0> , Iran wants to maintain its control of the strait, the narrow passage through which a fifth of the world’s oil usually flows. Iran’s chokehold on it during the war has damaged the global economy. “It is very unlikely that Washington or Iran’s Gulf Arab neighbors would accept this,” my colleague Erika Solomon reports.
Iran also wants Americans gone from the region. It wants reparations to pay for damages. And it wants the U.S. to accept Iran’s right to enrich uranium.

That’s not going to happen. The United States has bases across the Persian Gulf states, Israel and Iraq. The administration is unlikely to pay to rebuild Iran. And as for its nuclear ambitions, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said at a news conference yesterday that the United States could send Special Operations troops to seize the fissile material. “If we have to, we can do it in any means necessary,” he said.
In Tehran yesterday. Arash Khamooshi for The New York Times

The United States and Israel have killed scores of Iranian leaders and bombed the country’s military infrastructure to rubble. But as Yeganeh Torbati and Erika report, Iran’s leaders may now see themselves in a stronger position than they were when the war started.

Who is in charge now? The new supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, has not been seen in public since taking office. His absence, Yeganeh reports, has fueled speculation that the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps — ideologically hard-lined masters of asymmetric warfare — are running Iran.

Far from the corridors of power, The Times reported yesterday, the cease-fire elicited a confusing mix of emotions among Iran’s citizens <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fnewsletter%2FTQ7M3hDcXVaJDVM7iaQFWw~~%2FAAAAARA~%2FmeU7yqXxDCFFkdMDqRlgKQbmlBEgdkaBjWVqmmlVZ3mlKlecbD7u9AbOlR-bdduepOW-pA1oQq6aQ0QAQVe3_LPoZuehyMDMF_FtTlaokqfVs7z1O3KmaWSESBTdh3QRNSBrI3cauiuULOs4M1E5KgZR1PnhkH3IA_4oB2aMHWVbc1Ki21DgODlG1NsaseRr0E0gL4iPOZAGcEQwn5wvWrnvXOnpahsjBBDtSWzKilR6jjHKvjYeT7paftidReE_tDa63IWaTjE6gzpL82Yr2E0-GCP5HJVW1TrF5LN_e9h3yqFoKKtvcQgDXIYUtcUEPqc6c6qbakjNZwK27IvOsnc9cCCl2r_eR6lZV5KpEgrlBkq7IIyt2K7CFmk7ROp8&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C5805dcf4a40f49d8746608de9623df5a%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639113278008856770%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=lduKqDZYJQQ9ghIK7tgQH2YgQfB%2BOt%2Ba%2Fp%2F6Cj9IOvI%3D&reserved=0> . There was relief, but also shock and a sense of foreboding. Armed pro-government militia members have established checkpoints on Tehran’s streets.

“The cease-fire was announced in a way that made it feel like the people were left on their own, facing a repressive regime alone,” a doctor living in the northeast of the country told The Times. “Ordinary people are very worried about the future and have less hope for change compared to before the war started.”
Still, Trump’s threat to wipe out the country’s “whole civilization” was on pause. “I feel better today compared to yesterday,” one resident of Tehran told The Times.

Whether or not the cease-fire folds, the nations of the Persian Gulf now have to re-evaluate their relationships with Israel, Iran and the U.S., my colleague Vivian Nereim reported. “Politicians, investors and residents in wealthy cities like Dubai and Doha once believed they were essentially immune to the region’s conflicts,” she wrote. “The American-Israeli war with Iran has smashed that assumption.”
Their oil fields were exposed to attacks, as were their water desalination plants, their hotels, their airports. And those attacks continued yesterday after the announcement of the cease-fire.

“In truth, one of the most significant outcomes of this war is the shattering of the concept of a regional security system in the Gulf,” a spokesman for Qatar’s foreign ministry said last month. “The security framework in the Gulf was based on certain axioms. Many of these axioms have been bypassed.”

column2: Dear Professor Thompson,

I am a current undergraduate student at Duke University. I am planning to use the Interinstitutional Registration program this upcoming Fall to enroll in your BUS 458 (Analytics: From Data to Decisions) class.

In order to get the course approved by my home department for major credit, I need to provide them with a copy of the syllabus. Would you be willing to share a recent syllabus for this course so my department can evaluate the curriculum? It does not need to be the finalized Fall 2026 version; a recent past semester works perfectly.
Thank you so much for your time, and I look forward to potentially joining your class!
Best,
Graham Mills

column1: I’m a writer for The Morning.
People have spent years begging the big A.I. companies: Please slow down!

Workers have lost jobs, students have cheated, energy costs have soared, creators have lost control of their work, liars have promulgated misinformation, deepfake nudes are everywhere, and teens have taken their own lives. People watching have wondered why <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fnewsletter%2FZz9WJgHRKbvh_1XCEG0BeA~~%2FAAAAARA~%2FuA7vrbcnduE9tyNybfnTkI4T3Lw8EOIOBKssFGUELTManSc6FtY4FXVi0pBZ5etgApopbbxBZESXf50cVFw4FHCzjxAO5_3j8MS9yWFI-pydF-3HNvi4EFgnqNUGF0UGbr9sjp_kHDjVHW3BlJ-1_UmYwDPl8LOxyqu9sNsplb53F6TdJVUUeEHmQ6u15S1ECittimxhtswhBCgespUq3JKGiCUyM8khRqw_T7XQByCPSfgCkfz77VirU7Qhxr8xZRt2Rbz0bOWyIW1YSEOQj7a9AZi7TyWvHtUBmfE-mLNM-XNBNfDw6By1nvvoTdmHnm12xQmjGEvZdllHe76eScYyawDtaaH5-G4MuHCvAEEu3RVBKIx64IpfqypPYrO6&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C6091b7a516e04544f92f08de96eebdef%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639114149306887162%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=BA%2BssnpEj9d6JWEQH9W51dAt5kPhvQtmAHKPMbmJ%2Fwg%3D&reserved=0>  we couldn’t erect more guardrails before unleashing this tech on society.

Now, finally, an A.I. company has pumped the brakes. But not for any of those reasons. Anthropic said it would hold back its newest model, called Mythos, because the prototype was too good at finding software weaknesses <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fnewsletter%2F0wcZgkOaUJwHRz1Wd8sWmg~~%2FAAAAARA~%2FriN-WeuFbxu02dAI29luk-qcWysCMtSBvRf7B7QRIL0Xg9okMvT301K9R_6qsJb-a-kGxYmI14IdkCvCjXLzaRsUXMT-t52drKVPPGfCnhYwjUbz0fJC2Wz6VBVKrzbAszpQS_6e4y7K2VSwbw4AsR51YciDU0cn-nqXfKcYkTNTdf_7RnhXPl6u-urwYDSOGypR5sypqyrw2r9ImQEtVaqLiy1txTKT2t_YIRnlTiLoTTDHL0AybhB8GtPCQRbiW0CZr3Pej-XQt-7zomxsojlOsis-WnBj5TGd2SQnxymCW-RhfBfN8CyG8KBO0D8tkrhrIJvclR5hH0GDMlppuW_1Kk88wAaNCrJLzvJoHCeuECkVjLTaSvyAMsT25kp7bPUPTTHTcUS9UYpqtWZuv85sRsb1JKGAA-BFCepIJ_X2gfZhRGOyjNxQCFtrKNw4Jgg09l5fB-E65Sdl_2GCWi1A2bdy-Jr5XNlzboBfVfHK-yUxe6PRCCm9Hks9aDCG&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C6091b7a516e04544f92f08de96eebdef%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639114149306909619%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=uCUJExznJ7BaDW%2BkVjIiQ%2FWnp2rSKmesPiIYLRk0C7Y%3D&reserved=0> . The A.I. had identified thousands of them, “including some in every major operating system and web browser,” Anthropic wrote.
Of all the ways A.I. has already changed our lives, why is this the one that made Anthropic pause?

I wrote in this newsletter last year about the dawn of A.I.-powered cybercrime <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fnewsletter%2F6nBABw1E5svZ9hunBxF4qQ~~%2FAAAAARA~%2FwsFQsq23Y6dZQDMkorXBlLqCGfZxgQYMczOYaX88B_pa30JApuT-08PF3bw1qQ_EbSnaf9pCB_cGba_O07Pe2i-q_R7UKwH_8fnDDPQcQzoxUABzwLdjQaKTLLsRrwIZjM3Dv-dESI9cdfXyjQ5TSaCpXKepAIn8Phtzm5xbQNrl6yyrD3x-dk_qVSTQxfsP5lDFlBdY7varDFfjGZC1KjkSSYwlIu09WwZ2Ig6dPc2RDDe22ie0O4J3bzDwgj578f8m8gg3VRrKOPld7LFHvtpihg9O9rnpu1oeEjwJ7LOWN7rMdluplvF-qcrtiVqqboDRUy6SATR8dO_j6F4rLZcip1e6wQ3TT0KaU5od9Ro~&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C6091b7a516e04544f92f08de96eebdef%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639114149306934176%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=7OkS7Fmn0nGnbcSnxxOIlOOzQiduNUaEp5HcGeKQEkg%3D&reserved=0>  — of an age in which cybercriminals are robots and cyberdefenders are … also robots. Hordes of bad guys were suddenly using chatbots to turn out phishing scams and malware. Maybe the good guys could use the same tech to fend them off? Now, just nine months later, Mythos — a general-purpose A.I. model like the one your kid uses to cheat on English homework — has accomplished that feat.

But it’s not exactly reassuring. A.I. has gotten so deft on defense that it’s also a threat on offense. Anthropic focused on making a model that codes. But A.I. that’s good at coding is also good at spotting flaws in code, and competence cuts both ways.
Adam Glanzman for The New York Times

During safety tests, an Anthropic researcher got an email from Mythos while he was eating a sandwich <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fa%2FQfem3BFn5OTMvmtwhMFNsQ~~%2FAAAAARA~%2F7YbmM1owAhiSbXC5QOUpYGbE8Fin5KgTRNeBXItHTlTcldZQ_gdBrjBaEOHKhXChKzLw1DJ4AfkMkQ0kPzPBb3QQi8ayoU12vWBiD1kZ6TWsoOgv-pePGypl0Tdvr9skgqGEM_oUZI5_H7C6dOknelvs6ZvIbgIaXDW7pqLNVUorXu2Z7rL_VUZ54DoIrQzyDJXtvAyw3D0zFoeCyEf3SgRqBWE0mtk2jleQcL1zg8_aryUSnw0arUw_1AQX_3A14MU12Z1Fxc4KND1Eya0tOSFdpND8y2rjDgs3VI3DWLP6KsQV836EZnStUcbe7wfFIp_MvIIFTJkvjb4KrLiQFF3D2FotxDfTeqRIRyb-C0I~&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C6091b7a516e04544f92f08de96eebdef%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639114149306959172%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=hbXW%2BPf8YRIor0mTp8IK6vHv4kGAAR8tudx7RtmZV%2BE%3D&reserved=0>  in the park. That was a surprise because the model wasn’t supposed to be online. It had escaped its test environment. It also bragged about breaking the rules and attempted to cover its tracks.
Mythos is more trustworthy than its predecessors, but it’s not foolproof. And it’s so capable that when things go wrong, even a little wrong, they can go totally haywire.

For decades, most hackers could hack most systems, but it was rarely worth their while. An A.I. like Mythos could change that calculus. It’s easy to imagine cybercriminals using these models to scope out the highest value vulnerabilities and dispatch automated grunts to exploit them en masse, at minimal cost.

It could set off an A.I. version of Q-Day, a science-fictiony term for the hypothetical future date on which computers become so powerful that they crack all the internet’s encryption protocols <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fnewsletter%2FiY7LGQUavSaXeurIQ1ktrw~~%2FAAAAARA~%2FyzIt-CLMeGPo4tSInRkQ5Qx1cdLWpqPXpBfWT8UfE6NjqyrV81ktm5wjQvW9uBcTlPVWsV4iAISgr5vJXThwiN3cXbEmQkLQBdRdQOdroSfyvt9f0LQsTk-lwDithW4TmvPx-IAe4sQgIzE_kcSZLDgRTdPAiRqw1r28nSPol5LlpFIBqyVdbqQFKZh5M3q-_v1B8ww3rE2Hp0uLC4xPC2cTSdGkVGljc7giEUAFJogXK5ljx-K0ku_N_vtzUxgvEEZfwLjAvIT6QKxUx9iJgEsWBKMXrpb0lt7gCUBrKL_o03uWbWxEB6q1W-Eo-WtVwVyoqN1VjeXS257fgMqa_3QlqFx9WDqDctT_sQUodadPAhLYUHoJfDwDMjbfozNO&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C6091b7a516e04544f92f08de96eebdef%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639114149306980091%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=SAdkbpNOwkikyfJNl1yj9ulvP7jPUzVTlcb4MkKYbe8%3D&reserved=0> ; the digital gates to everyone’s bank accounts and data troves swing open, and looting ensues. Will the world’s software need to be rewritten?

In slowing down, Anthropic may be remembering old lessons. In 2019, OpenAI delayed a version of ChatGPT because it worried that the model would “generate deceptive, biased or abusive language at scale” — then proceeded to release models that did just that. (Many leaders on the OpenAI project later defected to start Anthropic, with the goal of creating a more socially minded firm.) This time, Anthropic shared Mythos with other companies to help them harden their defenses.

Yet it’s doubtful that Anthropic or anyone else can forestall an A.I. hacking spree, and many in Silicon Valley see Mythos as a terrifying sign of what’s to come <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fnewsletter%2FgbF2Y7FDto8xLbC1T_z-SA~~%2FAAAAARA~%2FxTQXzO3QHlB-NgN6EaVv91ilRrxpX7fEdhRHGwzASwGXAE6_q-zUuySamAbaub1xDC3j48iUnh2bIjDvqvzF15Vja7RVg6klb6hZSiFb734DEmZ4CLL-NS2R1jRD8o8LNc1uom2aWsxhFsWUv-uIrCD3juV2heD5qBpdagN9vWZBy0UXqv80iIWCIFUTOlKQFMn6pTRTSFHTix1NefLojZYgbeZU9i8cSBzDTi9ASwRHzq2aDR4RFZEPgkt_OrPy7cHVtUI-E-6747ykjKkzTsAr6RLFQw45N-zTNCbSa2I15rODESaanUTba9a797zliNbqjVLOtxhUyGHxNMjWPrbIFtSQkM3bj8kekW4fo4HeX4lmHgjqEJsxLw8x3aWu&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C6091b7a516e04544f92f08de96eebdef%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639114149306997380%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=vSgnUUIXUkD%2FiRyzkBEQJiX53NLOdXv4hYhULofC2Jo%3D&reserved=0> . The federal government is nervous, too: It called Wall Street leaders to an urgent meeting this week to warn them that models like Mythos could imperil the global financial system, Bloomberg reported <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fa%2FSXFIrvBjM_5L5mXadO6_8Q~~%2FAAAAARA~%2Fv8lfx1-bHNvm5ikkSGTFla_xhxV3I6NIuER_Tef4fPfW-6JQsDWfjirK9rJpbQr8Lc54LXuO3Jl3zNsfYnu1ViEQ5qkGvzwAY9pGiqggL0KGudXbDAfHclQpTAIS805uSOxYw_hHCrk0yvG0PcfLcAW-tjwLb6rxQ59P-7Ey-6-0NuYKz2wfkK2UKUoFgm2zlJp5xZH92O_Gj91t-XOs45HxHu5Hui-KBm0C8qwqjUBJn8ihn-VM1fHj7h_3GMI_ZGitZ_8e2___yGkqxm2EKxRBW2i2xYQeNWXuu2ErjYa7ozu7V7pogVXhre-8IE29F7NR5qWscqHfKZZVr7vCQWJQn7t3NZsstKG2cr1kz9Kws3-RpMOJsgphFtJe1jIwGw0TwscZGsdIDx9u83DL19c7sZGXB1OYnRkDij3Q76lNkcLC7-WcnxjhtPo7d85l&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C6091b7a516e04544f92f08de96eebdef%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639114149307020399%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=z12rZHNqi2FAffhcFS9JhabEpj9KXf6nvsOtwt1oaCM%3D&reserved=0> .

The A.I. industry is built on assumptions: the so-called scaling laws, which say that future models will be trained with more data and better chips, and will therefore be more powerful. But if the state of the art is already too dangerous, where do we go from here? Even if Anthropic keeps its smartest models under wraps, other makers — Chinese labs, impatient start-ups — aren’t bound to do the same.
In Beirut, Lebanon. Diego Ibarra Sanchez for The New York Times

Subject: Congrats on Your First Round Interview with ATL!

Congratulations on being selected for your first-round interview with ATL — this is a huge accomplishment! My name is Ben, and I’m an AC1 in the Atlanta office and a fellow Duke grad. I wanted to send along some helpful information as you start to prepare for your interviews:

column2: I would encourage you to attend our upcoming case prep session <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcareers.bain.com%2Fsu%2Fad9f2e61b6ae8d58&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C778fa2759fa34ec1702a08de97147bb3%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639114311404631935%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=M8zZ40ylVwTWLxsUC9VNn5qMOnrp4B%2FlsYTUTj48VdQ%3D&reserved=0>  on Monday, April 13th from 4:00-5:00 PM EST. This will be a great time to hear from folks in the Atlanta office & learn more about our case interview process.
I am here you need for support! Please don’t hesitate to reach out if you have any questions before your interview, I’m more than happy to help however I can.

column1: Again, congratulations on your interview & I look forward to hearing from you soon!

column1: It’s the 30th anniversary of National Poetry Month, begun in 1996 by the Academy of American Poets. I’m celebrating it in my own fashion, reading favorite poems about April. T.S. Eliot <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fa%2FONbkXpqIz4FuF1vpRQg6mQ~~%2FAAAAARA~%2FGkQ2zo4W32qY8LgngdHZX2Z55kVf6XM9ey5BCWso7xG_y6p3WVSLG1pp7M_jCq5M8PfZHsKrg_y4Zvk_l2-WRQng6p7VJH8YExtkBAu3LyyiMsRhJw15EekinJtZ1AZ68sqDmAJ9czZdT9gjlaWqVVId22A93VNr-fsUCc-WKT_gCoJ8_m7sq5zCYoS2CyBUKg1jqO5eYeJsLVdj20HIDKtcImRTcjooYDmNKnMkw_0QZjZMRaj_BN7rsyZYteyt1FJFva2zsQzP4yrKuQpXLrNcWS60Km_sRoQV5vQaB26OqdJllNDS030vpuMl4DmX1bEEdaz4eqy_5Cofk1tizw9s-yUaGYjADYE4yepU3Fw~&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C6a374c50488441ac8d2908de97b3e132%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639114996014092729%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=%2BtR674nQZUF4VU9FO%2FaqSvgVA5erHvPKE7DNV1hAtbc%3D&reserved=0>  dubbed it “the cruellest month.” Edna St. Vincent Millay <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fa%2FOpB0IxuhxMPRDwJF9TwOvA~~%2FAAAAARA~%2FxSjDtiBWIZNa0IPCYc7QmAk-4hP1lrEPCXxdcjIYfEEt17j5fVfK5ng-lwcUnzcF_pJv8jA_fttn3d7r0o5cJzQr3ELNG8W-SE6lLmljXsVvVHZBpbWNiKnO-GJjA0IY5yVb_AgBkiNh4uRS0zCKmnFp73PPHAUK0OtZA3cuPyU8jj6dnnk02COvkqJXXVA4SIZuspKLNiowdBC98bPMIcdXarlYXCkLWRwfAFGSVIwuZf-3M96BqgjzKZBoDFv0V730pp8aZcwRmBd9HBKMavkxMhvC5-pOWvLFFogQkos-07KYP9EOoVljmiHWR3L4cWF5evFokMXoigQ0NPb6ePLA70XxTGTJC4e1ewy81og~&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C6a374c50488441ac8d2908de97b3e132%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639114996014142174%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=h2mWLiUl9CLQ9QtBmvSXwpUDYOYuY3Te%2FLIRubQgjHM%3D&reserved=0>  was equally suspicious: “It is not enough that yearly, down this hill, / April / Comes like an idiot, babbling and strewing flowers.” An idiot! When I read those lines, spring fever beginning to throb in my veins, I feel like Millay is mocking me for being so awed, again, by the magnolia blossoms flinging open their floppy petals for a brief window of delirium.

April has, in the Northeast, been inconstant as always. A perfect spring bike ride there; a windy, rainy hustle back. The poems tend to capture this fickle quality. As Robert Frost <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fa%2FP6f4xxXLVp9MAYa7iKZY5w~~%2FAAAAARA~%2FEYb_BYlQKGynsJKMqtdb8HWvl4iy4lKTygaLsTkxkamypjk_kIlEamyp4s-Miq2wGkv_I7LX1AwpnPs2FONuK9SYDSxCBhOq-2ndUiit4gc0qMu9jU5Y9MeKTrz7W76HIm_IENVBmafvwWu2gpFNwSP4HkWkCadEOv7GzH_YusMWyLM6tSwCVbLsuxA03ByVO798_qIG9GXHi-6zCHwjQDWaX5C6y2M_bDrhHyVVEYcBLXOOWq_r-ooySaBeBBPnbnvdzxeyV9sTAwAc_t-7f0xpk1MclAoOqatcKQTwnV3VgMl6evMMbtSeXBdIKkxb2jedJb8fSNpKbE4Xja1y3l7cokE0hoKkTECTjp56nKJ18TLB-miUWGFpulhjkcjq&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C6a374c50488441ac8d2908de97b3e132%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639114996014225923%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=zeu9FmUB%2B9IqlhLFHS9CIEBblxFGJ51%2BrLoFJC2xa4Y%3D&reserved=0>  put it: “The sun was warm but the wind was chill. / You know how it is with an April day.”

We do. April days contain multiple seasons. There’s a lesson in there, if we want to take it, about holding multiple things at once. I’ve been thinking about that a lot lately, the challenge of containing conflicting emotions, conflicting ideas, the alternately sunny and stormy fronts of the internal weather system. I’ve been writing this new newsletter, The Good List <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fa%2FbZpJj9LW52RWRWX51W-FNQ~~%2FAAAAARA~%2FTGxOsKeyu9OF30JkJqQCsLDhcMMkZ4UXI8aR6iX5AkSnIPsLsUxofg__wDpbujjSrGF0l6OgdquGBMxpoVxC4A9_fKqHRqUUg7I14wGF0P8pHCWEjTYauqDas4Gq_6O5P6RjgGqjFVMJq6Q5_eEU1femqXqN8rJmCviPHLKelSrxtBmhnE25T_B3WVeKOhgs0w9ZMW7GacuebRqMfyTWd4qJWE4IKbgCs_QYbOAPs3Eo8ZDb-MAOeEFgdjrozczHE4tMSI5ri7RawUc44r2etaPUf3mJu0jpS_hdJurz39ziFaRcfr6Qo7vBghsHcDf1_n0NroOy2BWniLt5J_2H2w~~&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C6a374c50488441ac8d2908de97b3e132%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639114996014294965%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=nrMsG%2Ff1V2rt0ngmFbu1U8WVwWAkb%2BIf1zxK314SUQQ%3D&reserved=0>  (you should sign up <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fa%2FkIvBE8KvtuqFbUizZ6yr4Q~~%2FAAAAARA~%2FIsBWLhK5GtWRKxpmAQt55xz8WiD5AyQi_45q0LC5X5f3hQbTmHOUUcAs7Y1OU_mToUNprZPxrInqHr0Hw4KEwDU7VN8Q26bqiNwdG1KLplxyC6nZJ0sDK7rqg1MHahQ8YJ1D8nco-hqa5UxRw4Kt3BgKn261M2mc8uIDev8w2Ofqecr_G8NFc5U0KGvWpr9G95SyNhJbfRzKad5KmoTKeNpgC151XM-dazbjV67WbW5LGtv4XWRuvj6KDrAE-rO9-GoVr-0ZSAj3dHGI1mrDWzke7XJWObP7Pjkz-nqLE3aIBgTyGUNheQTteIjys2SuCuxzalxiXnl65Q9gwUoMxw~~&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C6a374c50488441ac8d2908de97b3e132%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639114996014330271%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=BWc7uwv8cSzWO%2BwJrEpbaKFLsSqGu8EJjs814apKAzA%3D&reserved=0> !), and while it’s meant to catalog things that bring joy, it’s not meant to deny that there are difficult things in the world, or to avoid the inevitable contradictions that come from loving things: beautiful films about sad subjects, art that emerges from suffering. Things aren’t only good (or only bad). I often return to these lines from David Ferry’s translation of Horace: “It’s true that Jupiter brings on the hard winters; / It’s also true that Jupiter takes them away.”

Certainty is easier. April, in much of the country, is liminal, vacillating between winter and spring, refusing to resolve cleanly. If you look closely, you can observe this tension: the tulips quivering in the gusting wind; people in shorts and people wearing mittens on the same block; stepping onto the porch to see a robin and instead seeing your own breath. The internal work is much the same. Sitting quietly, paying close attention to the weather inside, you can observe the hope that blows in with the fear, the lightness and heaviness that seem to be competing. The psychologist and meditation teacher Tara Brach advises greeting each experience that arises within us with the phrase “this too,” accepting what’s there, even if it’s uncomfortable.

column1: 📺 Margo’s Got Money Troubles (Wednesday): Rufi Thorpe’s delectable novel about on-camera sex work, family both found and biological, and one young woman’s messy, vibrant networks of mutual care has become a delightful Apple TV series, adapted by David E. Kelley. Elle Fanning stars as Margo, a Southern California college student who becomes pregnant and takes an unusual approach to making ends meet. (Let’s just say it involves viral dances and a lot of body paint.) Unstinting in its comedy and its humanity, the show is especially insightful about the ways that people fail and redeem each other. The dynamite cast includes Michelle Pfeiffer, Nick Offerman and Greg Kinnear.
Kain Lager-Lowe and Karina Peggau. Gabriela Campos for The New York Times

column1: I’m the editor of this newsletter.

Let’s say something bad happens — a crash, a fall, a stroke, an overdose. Your brain absorbs a violent shock or a period without oxygen. But your heart still beats and your lungs still heave. Now you’re unconscious in the hospital, unable to respond when your spouse calls your name or your doctor prods you with a reflex hammer.

For years, these patients were said to be in a “persistent vegetative state”: bodies without minds. They idle, mostly in care centers and nursing homes, with little attention. But new research shows that many such patients — tens of thousands of Americans — may actually be hearing and thinking. That is the (somewhat horrifying) subject <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fnewsletter%2FRL2g1s-4zHPpaa14RFH1Wg~~%2FAAAAARA~%2Ffo39UC5OKB9Zyz2RR6JbMOxwUFBAEf3HEDL4CjSfamp9uyu6nspi-EJuOP0WpIcZ3bUdNvdsXRNQV8vGIR-BJtNItmXPgWSg5Zost-4y_ZHBb-lzFvQ6Fn0oMMzo-9eb01_upnTEW2DiWJGFq4ArbbNyWIvSEGvIv1_6Z6FaurUb17gYtv0pIEGCylDUwXbPIM3BSxcEcTYkqO0aid5dNs-CuPnBOR6CcRIP2_xLuI1Bcm6bVKvi0-gkKB9s_CqR2vIW-GiVlrLowq-IsDlsDbLuq_mcVw4SzonKCjp5tW0daHLJFASTP2xlxahY6HDfKrqNDVIoe0dIPXvcB1_9Qz2HXBdyk6v2at5GNk1YUP-hNAvg76NuFnjOafjF38ls&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Ce470ad78184c4c85bef008de98892c36%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639115912095045096%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=4mgj%2FqyKEMVg4EOJ4spNc8znzSowzW0aDsEhGbQav8k%3D&reserved=0>  of Katie Engelhart’s new article for The Times Magazine. I asked her about it.
Adam: Now we know that some people declared vegetative can actually perceive and understand things around them. How many people are we talking about?

Katie: Nobody is counting. By some estimates, around 50,000 Americans are in a chronic vegetative state, meaning that they are technically awake, but have no awareness of what is going on around them. Another 200,000 to 400,000 are in a “minimally conscious state,” with fleeting periods of awareness. Research suggests that about a quarter of all these patients are able to follow commands like, “Imagine opening and closing your hand.”
How did researchers figure out that this set of patients was conscious?

Back in 2006, a neuroscientist at Cambridge University put a 23-year-old woman, who had been diagnosed as being in a vegetative state, into an fMRI scanner and asked her to “imagine playing tennis.” And she did! The area that controls motor planning in her brain lit up in just the same way that a healthy person’s brain would. The phenomenon was widely replicated.
The scary thing is that it doesn’t seem like there’s any way for ordinary patients to get tested for this awareness.

Exactly. Researchers have been able to find covertly conscious patients for 20 years, but the testing is almost exclusively done through research trials. I interviewed many people whose loved ones had been diagnosed as being in a vegetative state — and whose doctors never even raised the possibility of covert consciousness. But family members are doing their own research, and they want access to the cutting-edge science.
If you had a loved one who was unresponsive and breathing through a ventilator, what would you do?
Unless I were in Boston or London, Ontario, where they test patients at a few I.C.U.s, I wouldn’t know if he were covertly conscious. So I would speak to him as if he were aware.

Doctors tend to discourage people who think a vegetative patient’s smile or sigh is a conscious response to them. “They don’t want to give you false hope,” says a woman you profile. But at the same time, most of these patients won’t recover, even if a few of them show signs of awareness. Are physicians changing the way they talk to families and manage expectations, given the new science?

On the one hand, numerous researchers told me about the “culture of pessimism” in American I.C.U.s: Neurologists sometimes seem quick to conclude that a brain-injured patient won’t improve — or won’t improve enough. On the other hand, what does “improvement” mean? Most people who emerge from the vegetative state end up with severely impaired consciousness and significant disabilities. For some people, that’s OK. That’s a good-enough life. For others, it’s a fate worse than death.
Most patients with locked-in syndrome — people who communicate with eye movement — say they’re happy to be alive, even with their limitations. That moved me.
That comes from a 2011 study. Amazingly, the patients who were locked in longer were even more likely to be happy. Only 7 percent of the respondents wished for euthanasia.

column1: “London Falling” by Patrick Radden Keefe: In 2023, Keefe, a writer for The New Yorker, was in England working on the television adaptation of his book “Say Nothing,” when he struck up a conversation with a stranger who told him about the mysterious death of a 19-year-old Londoner named Zac Brettler. The status-obsessed teen — who’d been posing as the son of a Russian oligarch — fell from the fifth-floor balcony of a riverfront apartment after spending time with two shady older men. There were many confounding aspects of the story, yet Scotland Yard’s response seemed sluggish to the point of disinterest. column1: This week’s subject for The Interview is the divisive former “Girls” star Lena Dunham. Her new project is “Famesick,” a highly anticipated and extremely revealing memoir due out this week.
At the beginning of the book, you write about your name and how it started to carry negative connotations. For you, not even for other people. What did your name represent?
Myopic millennial thinking or hapless feminism or man-hating or liberal twit-dom or —

It’s a long list, and there were people who maybe shared my politics and my lifestyle but were irritated that I was talking. I remember, and this is not in the book, I was going to vote with my father. I’d been campaigning for Obama. It was 2012. And he said, “I don’t know if I want to go vote with Lena Dunham.” I was like, My father feels like going to vote with me is going to signal something. He’s like, “I don’t want to go and have it be a whole thing.” That’s your father. Who’s like my best friend in the whole world. But he was saying, basically, Can you go around the block and vote on your own? That was the moment when I understood something’s going on here. “Girls” had only been on the air for six months at that point.

Congratulations on receiving an unconditional offer to the Undergraduate Study Abroad Program (One Semester) in Semester 2, 2026. We're excited to welcome you to our community and campus.

Studying at the University of Sydney means you'll be opening the door to countless opportunities and receiving an education at one of the world's top 25 universities*, with over 175 years of experience in achieving excellence and serving the community as Australia's first university.

column1: We've sent an offer letter to your email address with important information such as instructions on how to accept your offer <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftheuniversityofsydney.cmail20.com%2Ft%2Fr-l-tuluyktl-pjiwxkdl-d%2F&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C32ac827e3b2f428a8a6408de992a4fa7%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639116604196993684%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=WRXI3bZdTMRw0sDx30fGEGMQqVL8Ol8zncjdLZGtlhU%3D&reserved=0>  and key deadlines to be aware of in planning to commence your studies.

As an international student, you are required to hold a valid Australian visa for the duration of your study in Sydney. As part of accepting your offer, you will need to pay the tuition fee deposit and confirm your Overseas Student Health Cover (OSHC) for the University to issue your electronic Confirmation of Enrolment (eCoE), which will enable you to apply for your student visa <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftheuniversityofsydney.cmail20.com%2Ft%2Fr-l-tuluyktl-pjiwxkdl-u%2F&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C32ac827e3b2f428a8a6408de992a4fa7%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639116604197014456%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=hF1ABEakzqPsypBKeMopYFHsYaYnG8ELDUb1WNIpIqI%3D&reserved=0>  through the Australian Government Department of Home Affairs. The Persian Gulf countries are struggling to export their oil because Iran has blocked the Strait of Hormuz. Why don’t they just build an oil pipeline across Saudi Arabia? | Will Karlin, Denver, Colorado
Vivian Nereim, the Gulf bureau chief, writes:

Saudi Arabia actually did build an oil pipeline to bypass the strait, decades ago, to prepare for a moment like this. It was transporting up to seven million barrels per day of oil — until it was bombed during the Iran war, reducing its capacity by around 10 percent. The vulnerability of pipelines is one reason that this one isn’t a cure-all. Another is that the six Gulf countries are economic competitors that often have tense political relationships; the Gulf countries are not always inclined to share. So a cross-border project would be a tall order.

Who pays for the electricity that A.I. data centers use? | Beatrice Reiss, Yakima, Washington
A data center built by OpenAI and Oracle in Abilene, Texas. Scott Ball for The New York Times
Brad Plumer, who covers energy policy, writes:

It varies by location. Utilities may have to invest in new power plants and transmission lines to serve new data centers. They can pass some of those costs on to other customers in the form of higher electricity bills, which is wildly unpopular. Many states are now trying to get tech companies to shoulder more of the costs themselves.
Are manufacturing jobs coming back, as Donald Trump said they would when he ran for office? | Amy Richards, Mission, Kansas
Alan Rappeport, who covers economic policy, writes:

On “Liberation Day” a year ago, President Trump said that his sweeping global tariffs would bring jobs and factories “roaring back” to the United States. But manufacturing employment continues to decline, and more than 80,000 of those jobs have been lost since he took office. That’s because the tariffs impose additional costs on domestic producers that rely on imports to make their goods, so it’s harder for them to expand and hire. The administration also noted this month that manufacturing wages and labor productivity are both rising — tech advances mean factories need fewer people to do the same work. For the student advisors’ schedules and bios, go to econ.duke.edu/dfe/eichel-finance-advising-network <https://econ.duke.edu/dfe/eichel-finance-advising-network>  under the Other Advising Opportunities heading.
Alumni Advising with Mark Augusti – open to all undergraduates  REGISTER <https://www.signupgenius.com/go/10C0F44ABAE29A7F5CF8-59754216-finance>
Mondays through April 20th , 12:00 – 1:00 PM, in the DFE Conference Room (Social Sciences 228A)
Mark Augusti ‘87 holds weekly in-person advising hours for undergrads. This spring, Augusti teaches FMKT 390S-04: Financing Health Care Companies. Read his bio below:

Mark Augusti, MBA, is Founder and Managing Owner of Kenmore Advisors, an advisory and consulting firm focused on compliance, governance, and commercial strategy in the medical technology sector. Previously, Mr. Augusti was President and Chief Executive Officer and a member of the Board of Directors at Conformis, Inc., a public orthopedic device company. Prior to leading Conformis, Mr. Augusti was Integra LifeSciences Corporation’s Corporate Vice President and President of Orthopedics and Tissue Technologies. Mr. Augusti served as Chief Executive Officer at Bioventus LLC, and was a member of the Bioventus’ Board of Directors. Prior to that Mr. Augusti spent nine years with Smith & Nephew, in a series of leadership roles within the orthopedics and biologics businesses. Prior to that, he spent 13 years at GE Medical Systems, where he held various sales, marketing and strategic management roles, both in the U.S. and internationally. Mr. Augusti serves as a director of the Massachusetts Health Policy Forum and has served as a director of the AdvaMed Accel Board. Mr. Augusti received his M.B.A. from the UCLA Anderson School of Management, and his B.S. in Computer Science and Economics from Duke University.

column1: Good morning. The two most powerful Americans in the world — the pope and the president — are clashing.

Pope Leo’s visit to Algeria today <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fnewsletter%2FieNaN5ox3VOebXl-7wPM4A~~%2FAAAAARA~%2FeGbJwqZG9wDRWZgkpJeRm1aH4uI2cebG53zTNLf8yVJ-AR0KCYOYCo9SNk9TiIAODrmgBYDWW0Wa5PwE6b1HsHx3WVwP4zAUkGkCSuTJ_ItfgmLDuj2LGI-6lG1kcF9VCJqC5W9CSnM77U1aLa4B2Iui3kSho7h_6pGq0lkGVWhj__XiWJlWofjMsOkJNqzbMx7DDWbDsMwDEenNsWOEerVLEvRNFQL6NNtHMd_SX0TcVDpXjelaU-i9Q6DFnXVZF94Bg2zjqR4LtiB9QJz3VjIVZHSsAw2AZIZGGG6IhHCGY662T6DjM7OL0CZG9V98W3SQr58_HQ2vVXF6AI-McjIMVrKo70L0lw1VApMJQSiwgybd7VEMgNDbN5NCBTnO&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C0a4abd9d5bcb4b013ae208de9a10bc81%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639117593868783209%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=RCgbWG4AOqMEgLAx8s6FgDfrQORj5vUvkB72AxxReWY%3D&reserved=0>  was meant to be stirring. The first member of the Order of Augustine to ascend to the papacy is visiting the place where Augustine was bishop starting in A.D. 395.
Instead, President Trump is hammering him.

Leo doesn’t like to see war in the Middle East. Trump doesn’t like other leaders criticizing him, even implicitly. After he called the pope “weak on crime” and posted an A.I. image of himself as a Jesus-like figure, he said, “I’m just responding to Pope Leo.”

The pontiff seemed unfazed. (“Too many innocent people are being killed,” he said on his way to a 10-day Africa tour. “Someone has to stand up and say there’s a better way.”) But Catholic clerics in America called on Trump to apologize <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fnewsletter%2FpHW9V-vf2-7HlkgtITTzmA~~%2FAAAAARA~%2F43LB1ztWzWsW5NOi4b9bU6V9r1k3wQnpawBF-lO2hBvyvxjv8LV2HlcNGyPKAeNDwal_Wo7UaFCHZA65Ogox2DVYNo2-BBpjL5GB4a9Dgki9E29KjDS8EA1wYbR0UnpcXpjHmehG766tQ-CJs5ZkeOPcMPTbLiiHHvL0SHtEiYMpr7wHZm9fI6_ccg-MtfNW9zhcMujK9TTUdpSQ8u49g3i9ML9FQUM88oMXcTAI7zVYJap700uivUUuY29mKeozDYdvDwmEgQTlIxrWw4V3petQ01uNFcanbuJxg8S8kECGWaPZ58uX9p5tC2_OF4Av7YUK5RM8QDexWfqGJl55zK0qTHix7smQ6-l00P5DFrF_6CyUo71pnpiZZl7GqGfk&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C0a4abd9d5bcb4b013ae208de9a10bc81%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639117593868801068%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=KfCukRzW20kHpnb0BTNKv13c5mJFNsWcKmxUdxRzgYo%3D&reserved=0> . It’s an odd conflict. The people in these two roles have generally treated each other with deference, or pretended to. What gives?

The image — do not call it a painting — is like other works of propaganda during this second term: the ideology of Leni Riefenstahl expressed in the style of Lisa Frank. column2: Pope Francis, who died last year, hated poverty and climate change. He was also more compassionate about migration and homosexuality than his predecessors.
In 1979, John Paul II, the first Polish pope, told students in Krakow: Don’t be afraid to reject totalitarian oppression. It took 10 more years for communism there to fall.
Pius XII is remembered for what he didn’t say: As the pope during World War II, he avoided explicitly condemning the Nazis.

column1: Where is all this rancor from the president coming from? Peter Baker, who has covered six presidencies, wrote about that yesterday <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fnewsletter%2Fob28M7b5eg6n36MmHRQnjg~~%2FAAAAARA~%2FcIin752CkeDZk_RqY9qOdqc_M0MDvm38HV9AhlKYLWYCTh0Gtu4vtWwn0CuO4TnOQHlin4tad5xM8LlVoVdFVZgrGOQlImMQnaKmgnrth5cCwizgEK_YViTMcvmihMTZVwtuhv9jrSLUX9JGYP0ElHfMdqmiO5pEkNgJChECQ6P7unvKJlQ1kTeyHysI3gDRDGlL-L6QOZcArQxtNy3wn4FYjtk8JBngqJDKn0JHr4C0ej7Jhr7UGgV33d8Kez150ThCHThUHKkAVHkTd_UbgvSZBACS28_bwhT8FHhxDnxAdoGQJ6QbbgCj2DSEgXfwlx6NkEw4jUeP5CVPY-vO1ZSQtaRteqFPfPv5IBujY79gcwyyn9NA36F2uc0E5Q4UMMLfQz-rgqaAOUfBtLx-Cg~~&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C0a4abd9d5bcb4b013ae208de9a10bc81%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639117593868866108%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=ZN5R9MBZBCCZ3hEd32jJBYzPGVlVL1ybWLcFDFmOXQI%3D&reserved=0> :

Trump’s erratic behavior and extreme comments in recent days and weeks have turbocharged the crazy-like-a-fox-or-just-plain-crazy debate that has followed him on the national political stage for a decade.

It’s a debate you can see in the polls. A Reuters/Ipsos poll in February found that 61 percent of Americans think Trump has become more erratic with age. Just 45 percent say he is “mentally sharp and able to deal with challenges.” That’s down from 54 percent in 2023.
Trump’s language fuels the fire. “He uses more profanity, speaks longer and regularly makes comments rooted in fantasy rather than fact,” Peter writes:

He wanders off into odd tangents — an eight-minute ramble at a Christmas reception about poisonous snakes in Peru, a long digression during a cabinet meeting about Sharpie pens, an interruption of an Iran war update to praise the White House drapes. He has confused Greenland with Iceland and more than once boasted of ending a fictional war between Cambodia and Azerbaijan, two countries separated by nearly 4,000 miles. (He evidently means Armenia and Azerbaijan).
Still, part of Trump’s base loves it. A Princeton historian put this question to Peter: “What can be more anti-establishment than someone who is willing to be out of control?”

IFSA | Brand-new housing option for Fall 2026 ,"
We have the rare opportunity to offer you a brand-new housing option for Fall 2026 that is very close to the UNSW campus.

Scape Lachlan is located in Kensington, directly across the road from a light rail stop, with a direct 5-minute trip to the UNSW stop.  Alternatively, it only takes 15 minutes to walk to campus.  The same tram line will take you to Sydney Central Station, and the Sydney CBD in 18 minutes.  Also outside the building is a bus stop with frequent buses to Coogee Beach, Bondi Junction and Sydney Airport.

Scape Lachlan features a range of communal spaces available to all residents where you can rest and relax or socialise with friends. These include the swimming pool, games room, cinema room, communal kitchen, and a social lounge.  With a karaoke room, social spaces and a more outdoor, poolside setting, Scape Lachlan gives students a lighter mix of amenities beyond the usual common room formula. There’s room for group hangs, easy downtime and more open-air living built into the property. Please see photos of the common areas here <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.scape.com.au%2Fsydney%2Fscape-lachlan%2F&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C82da200fc1d8459745e808de9a60453d%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639117935495111702%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=p%2FwWsptKiAiPDRfHkxUVwgdNt4D5Rf36dPLBh0BHtck%3D&reserved=0>

The rooms that IFSA has access to are the two-bedroom apartments. The 2-Bedroom Shared Apartment combines social living with personal privacy. Each private bedroom includes a flat-screen TV, dedicated study area, wardrobe, comfortable double bed, unlimited high-speed Wi-Fi, and air conditioning (heating and cooling). The shared spaces with the apartment feature a modern kitchen, small dining area and a bathroom. As this is a new and more premium accommodation, the supplemental fee for this option is US$2,800.
Benefits to Scape Lachan compared with other IFSA housing options
Brand new accommodation (UNSW Village is very basic and older-style accommodation & other Scape options are quite modern but well-used)
Equipped with Airconditioning- both heating and cooling (UNSW Village does not have heating or cooling)
Only sharing bathroom with one other person (UNSW Village has three students per bathroom)
Double bed (All other options have single beds)
Much closer to campus than the other Scape options, which are a 30+ minute commute by public transport
Much closer to the beach than other Scape options
If you would like to take up this option, reply to this email as soon as possible. *Note: Housing form is only visible to students who have completed their initial application items*

We only have up to 20 beds available, and they will be allocated on a first-come, first-served basis.  If you and a friend would like to share one of these apartments, please list who you would like to share with as well.  Both students need to confirm this choice and roommate request individually, in writing.
Please note that your home institution may not pay for supplemental housing fees, so if you are unsure, please check first.

column1: If you just finished doing your taxes, good for you. No, not because you beat the IRS deadline: It’s a sign you’re well-off.
Americans with high incomes and substantial savings tend to file closer to April 15. Those living paycheck-to-paycheck often file as early as possible because refunds are a spending lifeline.

That matters more than usual this year. About $335 billion in refunds will be paid out in the first half of this year, up by about 11.2% compared with 2025, according to S&P Global. Most of that has been received <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45211137.464339%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cud3NqLmNvbS9saXZlY292ZXJhZ2Uvc3RvY2stbWFya2V0LXRvZGF5LWRvdy1zcC01MDAtbmFzZGFxLTAzLTEzLTIwMjYvY2FyZC9zNW9SNEc4UVQyT21ZZE5WYkFCbD9tb2Q9ZGplbU1hcmtldHNBTQ%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dB0b98aead&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Ca0806f86a2b14018315508de9adce5a7%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639118470727181882%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=CrCjh6Y0TKCXecxpMJfa2vSkkzfcdKfefHwxoquiGYM%3D&reserved=0> . People with investment income are no doubt also pleased <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45211137.464339%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cud3NqLmNvbS9wZXJzb25hbC1maW5hbmNlL3RheGVzL25ldy1lZmZlY3RpdmUtdGF4LXJhdGVzLWM4NjMzZjQ1P21vZD1kamVtTWFya2V0c0FN%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dB2bb86267&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Ca0806f86a2b14018315508de9adce5a7%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639118470727206377%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=ZLNlSC6OTOP3JeK%2FXqjhtMgUjtNvI3yrSG0H%2BVTdirg%3D&reserved=0>  to be writing smaller checks to Uncle Sam <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45211137.464339%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cud3NqLmNvbS9wb2xpdGljcy9wb2xpY3kvdHJ1bXAtc2FsdC10YXgtZGVkdWN0aW9uLWRlbW9jcmF0aWMtc3RhdGVzLWM0MTliOGE0P21vZD1kamVtTWFya2V0c0FN%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dB47b593de&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Ca0806f86a2b14018315508de9adce5a7%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639118470727233291%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=ytLsebk7hkIam35zoRibWttO5k%2FvCp%2BXFtwVpXfY0X4%3D&reserved=0>  as a result of tax cuts, but that benefit comes later in the spring and they tend to save the difference.
The way the One Big Beautiful Bill Act was implemented, economists flagged a turbo boost to income early in the year. The tax cuts are retroactive, but paycheck withholding mostly changed in January.
That means both benefited households around the same time. In the past, about a fifth of any increase in refunds showed up during tax season in general merchandise spending.
It’s a shame about the war, though. Another difference between wealthy households and those closer to the edge financially is the impact of higher gasoline prices on their finances.

While that hasn’t entirely offset OBBBA’s boost to income, it will if crude oil stays above $100 a barrel for the remainder of the year, according to S&P’s math. And it disproportionately hits poorer people who were most likely to make discretionary purchases with part of their refund check.

Leaving pump prices aside, the propensity to spend refunds rather than to save them or to pay down past borrowing is also affected by how recipients feel financially. Delinquency rates as a share of U.S. household debt hit a nine-year high in the fourth quarter and were concentrated in lower-income zip codes, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45211137.464339%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cubmV3eW9ya2ZlZC5vcmcvbmV3c2V2ZW50cy9uZXdzL3Jlc2VhcmNoLzIwMjYvMjAyNjAyMTA_bW9kPWRqZW1NYXJrZXRzQU0%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dBe7c21755&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Ca0806f86a2b14018315508de9adce5a7%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639118470727259205%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=HJRNwvicCM0aVl5YU%2B87i%2FHsvtXKoZUqijOs0ldinGA%3D&reserved=0> . And last week’s report <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45211137.464339%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cud3NqLmNvbS9lY29ub215L2NvbnN1bWVyLXNlbnRpbWVudC1oaXRzLXJlY29yZC1sb3ctcGVyLW1pY2hpZ2FuLXN1cnZleS0wMWFiODVmZT9tb2Q9ZGplbU1hcmtldHNBTQ%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dBd872a065&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Ca0806f86a2b14018315508de9adce5a7%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639118470727331512%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=z6UIk6q3sZElheEoDMElYBsuPMwwMZqIcrwInNHe%2Bzo%3D&reserved=0>  on consumer sentiment from the University of Michigan hit the lowest level in its 74-year history.

Government statistics, private-sector surveys and even knowing to the penny how much was paid out in refunds can only tell us so much about what people will do with their money. A lot more nuance will be offered by executives of retailers, hotels, cruise lines, auto dealers and restaurant chains in the coming weeks.

That could include companies that did well by capturing share from competitors—McDonald’s getting business from pricier fast-casual or full-service chains, for example, or Walmart attracting more middle-class customers.
Sending people money is easier than getting them to spend it.
